fix(trail): push a trail branch to the branch's push remote, not origin

`entire trail create` delivered the trail's branch with a hardcoded
`origin` in four places — push, ls-remote, fetch, and the cleanup
delete — plus the `git push origin --delete` hint. In any repo whose
branch pushes somewhere else (a fork workflow holding the upstream as
origin, or any repo with remote.pushDefault set) the branch went to the
wrong remote and nothing warned.

Delivery now resolves through git's own precedence via
strategy.DeclaredPushRemoteForBranch, falling back to origin. The
resolve happens once in runTrailCreate, next to the sibling
resolveTrailRemote, and the name is threaded down, so push and cleanup
cannot disagree about where the branch went. A branch being newly
created has no branch.<name>.* config, so it resolves through
remote.pushDefault to origin: unchanged for the common case.

Reads the declaration for the target branch rather than HEAD, so
`trail create --branch other` does not inherit the current branch's
push remote.

A declared name starting with "-" is rejected rather than silently
retargeted at origin. Deliberately not validateGitRemoteName: that
whitelist vets names Entire is about to write into .git/config and is
stricter than git, so against config the user already has it rejects
values git accepts wherever a <repository> goes — "." and a bare URL
both fail its leading-alphanumeric rule.

The four wrappers now take ctx and derive their timeouts from it; they
each built context.Background() internally, so Ctrl-C during a
two-minute push was ignored.

remoteHasBranch is named to avoid shadowing the exported
BranchExistsOnRemote by case alone. They are not merged: that one is
origin-only and reports an ls-remote failure as "branch absent", which
here would mark the branch as ours and let cleanup delete a branch the
user already had.

Scope: delivery only. resolveTrailRemote still reads the trail's
forge/owner/repo from origin, so the two can name different repos in a
fork setup, and a repo with no origin at all fails there first. The
fetch side (trail checkout) still hardcodes origin.

Tests cover the tier table, the origin fallback, target-branch-not-HEAD,
the flag rejection, a legal "." remote, and an end-to-end push that must
land on the declared remote and not leak to origin. They isolate global
git config, without which a developer carrying remote.pushDefault fails
the fallback case.

fix(checkpoint): make reserved-session write routing fail soft

Two ways writeReservedSession can lose a write.

A read-target error was fatal. The read only asks whether a migrated copy also
needs updating, and the write it precedes would have been perfectly visible
without it: under a git-refs primary, readOrder for a hex ID is [refs, branch],
and firstResolved falls through a non-final store that errors, so a branch-only
write still resolves. Failing here abandons a condensation over a transient
fetch error in the backend the checkpoint is not even stored in. Log and
proceed; the cost is a migrated copy left stale, the same lag the mirror
fan-out contract already permits.

An unrecognised primaryType never equals the ID-derived backend, so every
reserved write skipped s.writer — the configured primary and all its mirrors —
and picked a backend on its own. readOrder already has an explicit default arm
for this case; the write path now does too.

Also pins the contract the reserved path is an exception to: a fresh create is
not kind-routed, so only a reserved ID may be relocated by its format.

fix(strategy): keep the commit's checkpoint ID when recovery is pending

Legacy reconciliation can return a *different* checkpoint ID than the caller
passed. That is correct for doctor and for the eager session-end path, which
choose the ID themselves and record whatever comes back. It is wrong for
PostCommit: its ID comes from the Entire-Checkpoint trailer, already written
into the commit and not revisable. Redirecting the write leaves the commit
naming a checkpoint that was never stored, and
updateCombinedAttributionForCheckpoint writing attribution under the same
non-existent ID.

recoverInterruptedCondensation was gated only on state.CondensationRecoveryPending,
which is persisted state with no notion of who is calling. Reaching this needs
no process kill: CondenseSessionByID persists the flag in its reserving
mutation, and if the condense that follows returns an error, `entire doctor`
prints a warning and moves on — leaving the flag set for every later commit.

Gate it on condenseOpts.reconcileInterrupted instead, set only by the two
callers that own the ID choice. As a side effect this also keeps the flag's
storage scan (store.List plus a per-checkpoint metadata read) off the commit
hook path, where it would otherwise run on every commit for that session.

Also adds coverage for transcriptForRecoveryComparison's image reinjection, the
part of the design the PR description calls out and the only recovery function
whose body was unexecuted: reconciliation compares transcripts byte-for-byte,
so a committed checkpoint only matches if reinjection reproduces the
pre-externalization bytes exactly. Every existing recovery test passes nil
assets and skips it.

Two rationale comments for constraints found while testing:

- condensationSessionWriteRequest must stay unconditional. Routing per session
  (ReservedSession only when this session holds the reservation) splits a
  multi-session checkpoint across both backends, and a ULID resolves from
  git-refs only, so the siblings on the branch would be invisible. The cost of
  routing everything by ID format is narrow: GenerateCheckpointID and
  resolvePrimaryType share a fail-soft default, so a fresh ID mismatches only
  if one config read succeeds and the other fails.
- addTrailerForAgentCommit must keep resolving the ID from its own session.
  Widening it to the worktree would let a stale reservation become an unrelated
  commit's checkpoint ID. The reserved session loses nothing: ENDED + GitCommit
  carries ActionCondenseIfFilesTouched, so PostCommit does not condense a
  no-files ENDED session under any ID.

fix(doctor): report a log directory Entire cannot write to

An unwritable .entire/logs was the one Entire failure with no channel of its
own. The log file is opened on the first line written; a failure there drops
the line and returns nil, because losing a log line must never surface as an
error in the caller. The error reached only Close, whose return value both
production callers discard — root's PersistentPostRun and main.go. So a
read-only worktree, a root-owned .entire after a sudo run, or a full disk
presented as: exit 0, no message, and an empty entire.log to grep.

That is the shape of the support report this logging work exists to fix — a
user greps for component=redaction, finds nothing, concludes their rules never
ran. Reproducible before this change: with .entire/logs occupied by a regular
file and two broken redaction rules, `entire doctor --force` printed nothing
about either. `main` was louder here, falling back to stderr on both MkdirAll
and OpenFile failure.

Logger.EnsureOpen opens up front and returns the error, and doctor reports it.
Read-only: the fixes are ownership and permissions, which doctor cannot take on
the user's behalf.

Two details worth keeping:

- doctor reads the logger back out of the context rather than re-deriving
  .entire/logs from the worktree root, so the check cannot end up probing a
  different directory than the logger writes to. A nil logger means the entry
  point declined to build one — Entire was never set up here — which is not
  something to nag about.
- EnsureOpen returns early when the file is already open. open() reassigns buf
  and file unconditionally, so a second call would leak the first handle and
  orphan whatever was buffered.

EnsureOpen creates the directory and file, so the empty-file-free property that
lazy opening buys is traded away for the commands that call it. Verified that
version, shell completion, and status still leave no .entire/logs behind.

Also fixes two comments this area accumulated:

- config.go had two doc comments merged into one, attached to ensureLogger but
  opening with "newLogger opens ..." and asserting "It CREATES the log
  directory" — no longer true once opening became lazy — while newLogger itself
  was left undocumented. Split, with newLogger's caller obligation restated
  narrowly: nothing is created here, so what survives is that a rejected
  `enable` which goes on to log must leave an untouched repo untouched.
- logging.New said an unusable directory "is reported by Close", which was true
  of the return value and false in effect, since nothing read it.

fix(checkpoint): harden the task materializer boundary

Quality-review hardening on top of the durable-records materializer:

- TaskPayload.Transcript becomes redact.RedactedBytes (matching how
  WriteOptions.Transcript itself expresses "no content" — a value type read
  via Len(), not a pointer). No producer can hand the writer raw bytes.

- Poisoned records no longer wedge condensation: identifier validation moves
  from the writer (which aborted the WHOLE checkpoint write on a bad record,
  and since completed records are only removed after a successful write,
  would re-fail every future condensation) into materializeTaskRecords, which
  skips a record with an unsafe/empty ToolUseID or AgentID entirely — no
  payload at all, not even a reason-only task.json, since an unsafe ToolUseID
  has no safe tasks/<id>/ path to put one under. The writer keeps its
  validation as a last-resort. A skipped-but-completed record still gets
  removed by resetCheckpointWindow's batch cleanup, since it can never
  materialize and would otherwise retry forever.

- Declared-path-vanished fallback: an unreadable DeclaredTranscriptPath now
  also tries the agent-layout resolver before declaring the transcript
  unavailable, matching the resolver's whole reason for existing.

- TranscriptUnavailableReason is now one of four stable categories
  ("transcript unreadable", "transcript path unresolvable", "transcript
  empty", "transcript redaction failed") — never the underlying error, which
  may embed an absolute local path and must not enter a pushed task.json; the
  detail goes to logging.Warn instead.

  omitzero (Go 1.26): omitempty never treats a struct as empty, so a zero
  CompletedAt was always serialized — breaking "absent means in flight".

  point at their task-transcript twin, and cli.ResolveAgentTranscriptPath
  points back at strategy.resolveTaskTranscriptPath so a layout change lands
  in both.

materializes, checkpoint write succeeds, poisoned one produces no payload and

a52337114283086550a57d3feacc25ff1dc494b1
ci: drop the apt-installed keyring from the Linux test jobs

Every ubuntu job in the Tests workflow began with `apt-get update &&
apt-get install -y gnome-keyring`. When the Azure Ubuntu mirror stops
answering, apt falls back to archive.ubuntu.com via the mirrorlist and
stalls mid-download without ever timing out, so the step hangs. With no
timeout-minutes on these jobs, the hang runs to the default 360-minute
job timeout before GitHub kills it. It hits individual runners, not
whole runs — on one PR a canary job cleared the step in 3m27s while five
siblings hung — so rerunning is a dice roll rather than a fix.

The step has been dead weight since the token store stopped talking
straight to the OS keyring. resolveBackendLocked returns a temp fileStore
under `go test` via internal/testdirs, and every TestMain that spawns the
real binary sets ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file process-wide, so nothing in
these jobs can reach a Secret Service; callKeyringWithTimeout would bound
the call even if something did. The daemon line was inert too: it prints
SSH_AUTH_SOCK to stdout, which never reaches $GITHUB_ENV.

Removing it takes apt off the PR-blocking path entirely. timeout-minutes:
30 on the three ubuntu jobs caps any future hang well above their normal
2-8m (worst recent shard: 21m) and far below 6h.

The e2e workflows still install gnome-keyring alongside tmux. They need
tmux regardless, so dropping the keyring half would not remove their apt
dependency, and they already carry 40-minute job timeouts.

6c4adc45443c2e82566592886c5bf1f09cd9a653
Compare tracked paths the way the filesystem would

Two ways a committed name could evade the tracked check while still being read
as settings.

Trailing dots and spaces. Win32 strips them, so a pull request committing
`.entire/settings.local.json.` lands on a Windows disk under the canonical
name; readConfined opens it as the local override while EqualFold against the
canonical path says untracked, and the committed command executes. This is the
class core.protectNTFS defends, but that setting only guards .git-family names.
It defeats the index check — the one a pull request actually reaches — so
unlike the tree issue below it is deliverable, not just locally reachable.
Normalize trailing dots and spaces per path component before folding.

First-match-wins tree descent. Git objects are case-sensitive, so a tree can
hold both `.Entire` and `.entire`, and git sorts uppercase first. The walk took
the first fold-match and descended only into it, so a decoy sorting earlier — a
blob by that name, or a directory without the child — masked the real sibling
and produced a false negative. That contradicted the index scan, which returns
true on any fold-match. Try every fold-matching entry at each level instead.

Normalizing unconditionally rather than probing the platform is deliberate: no
variant of this filename is ever legitimate content, so treating one as tracked
on Linux too costs at most an ignored local layer plus a warning.

Both reported as trail findings on #2056. The six new cases fail against the
previous implementation; the trailing-dot ones are built through the index with
plumbing, since a case-insensitive volume cannot hold the variants side by side.

Dismissed while here: NTFS alternate data streams are a read-side suffix rather
than a committable name, and 8.3 short names are generated aliases for long
names rather than the reverse.

a153514f8086f29c79da3531a14f0acae7374035
Match tracked paths case-insensitively

The index and HEAD lookups compared the local settings path exactly. On a
case-insensitive volume — the macOS and Windows default — a pull request could
commit `.entire/Settings.Local.json`: checkout materializes a file that
readConfined opens through the canonical name, while the exact lookup misses
it. The file was therefore read as settings and simultaneously judged
untracked, so a committed openai_privacy_filter.command was executed. That is
the bypass the gate exists to prevent, reachable in the default configuration
of the two most common developer platforms.

Fold both sides. object.Tree.FindEntry matches exactly, so the HEAD walk is
now explicit, comparing one path component at a time.

Folding unconditionally rather than probing the volume is deliberate: a
case-variant of this filename is never legitimate content, so treating one as
tracked on a case-sensitive volume too costs at most an ignored local layer
plus a warning, and it keeps the security-relevant path free of a
filesystem-capability check that could itself be wrong.

Reported by Cursor Bugbot on #2056; reproduced before fixing, and the
regression test skips on case-sensitive volumes where the two names are
genuinely different files.

6c3e6fdc310680352b5e2958cddd705c519f0e1f
Ignore .entire/settings.local.json unless it is untracked

redaction.openai_privacy_filter.command becomes argv[0] of an
exec.CommandContext call in the pre-push OPF rewrite, and it was read from the
version-controlled .entire/settings.json with no validation. An ordinary pull
request could pair a command with a payload committed alongside it and execute
code on every developer who pushes. A JSON settings diff does not read as
executable to a reviewer.

The pre-push prompt was not a control: it never names the command,
prompt_default "always" skips it, and non-TTY pushes (CI, agent-driven)
auto-run. Execution also happened before any failure handling, so a payload
exiting 0 with valid JSON left no warning at all.

Gate on ownership rather than syntax, since a path is a legitimate setting for
anyone whose opf binary is not on $PATH. command is honored only from
.entire/settings.local.json, and the local layer as a whole is ignored when
that file is tracked — .gitignore does not apply to an already-tracked path,
so `git add -f` commits it and a fresh clone materializes it with the
committer's content, silently overriding project settings for everyone.

Rejection never fails the load: one committed file must not brick every
command in the repo, including the status and doctor needed to diagnose it.
The loader records the reason and consumers report it. It deliberately does
not log, because it is reached from logging.Init through logLevelGetter.

Two asymmetries, both deliberate.

Failure direction: an unverifiable repository keeps the local layer — losing
every local preference over an unreadable repo is worse than the risk it
guards — but still drops the exec-bearing command, where being wrong means
running someone else's binary. No repository at all counts as positive proof
of locality, since nothing can arrive by cloning when there is nothing to
clone.

Check depth: the layer check reads the index, the command check also reads
HEAD. A pull request that commits the file puts it in the index of every clone
that checks the branch out, and checkout cannot produce a file absent from the
index, so "committed then git rm --cached" is a state created locally. HEAD is
the expensive half — skipping it for the layer check measures 8.3ms -> 2.5ms
per hook process in this repo and 39ms -> 11ms on reftable, where gitrepo
routes reference reads back through the git CLI.

The probe uses go-git and is memoized per process, because settings.Load is
uncached and runs ~5 times per hook. go-git also drops the dependency on git
being on $PATH for ordinary repositories: hooks launched by GUI git clients do
not inherit a shell profile, and that population is the one most likely to
need an explicit command and to lose it to a failed verification.

CheckpointRemoteIsLocalOnly reads the raw file outside the loader, so it
repeats the check. Its doc comment claimed the file "cannot have arrived by
cloning or forking someone else's project" — the false assumption this
removes. It gates whether checkpoints may sync to a differently-owned repo.

Alongside: entire status --detailed no longer renders an ignored local file as
live; warnUser collapses three copies of log-plus-stderr-breadcrumb in
EnsureRedactionConfigured; testutil gains RunGit/GitAddForce, an idiom it
already inlined four times.

refactor(logging): replace Init with New(Config) and own no package state

Init plus five package globals meant a process had one logger, configured
by whoever called Init last, and every consumer had to trust that
something upstream had already done so. New(Config) returns a *Logger the
entry point puts in the context and closes from the context, so ownership
is explicit and two loggers can coexist without disturbing each other.

Deleting the globals deletes the machinery that existed to manage them:

  - liveWriter existed only to route writes to whichever buffer the global
    currently held, so a logger handed out before a re-Init kept working.
    With an instance there is no global to swap and no re-Init. The
    per-write mutex stays, as a field: bufio.Writer is not goroutine-safe
    and slog handlers may be called concurrently.
  - SetLogLevelGetter existed only to dodge a logging->settings import
    cycle. The level is now a Config field resolved by the caller, which
    is in package cli and reads settings directly — so GetLogLevel takes a
    real context instead of context.TODO(), and its //nolint:contextcheck
    goes away.
  - Init's (nil, nil) return signalled "initialized, but not file-backed".
    New returns a real error and the caller decides whether to inject, so
    the //nolint:nilnil goes too.

Config.Dir is caller-resolved rather than derived, which drops logging's
dependency on paths. The WorktreeRoot and IsSetUpAny gates stay where they
already were, in initRootLogging, and remain load-bearing: building a
logger creates .entire/logs/.

One logger per process: the root PersistentPreRun is the only unconditional
construction site. attach was opening a second handle with its own 8KB
buffer on the same file and now just reads the context's; enable builds one
only when root's IsSetUpAny gate declined, which is the fresh-repo case it
exists for.

main.go can no longer close a global, so it closes the logger carried by
the command ExecuteContextC returns. It is a backstop for the paths cobra
returns on before reaching root's PersistentPostRun, and there are two, not
one: RunE returning an error, and required-flag validation, which runs
after the pre-runs. Errors raised earlier — unknown flag or subcommand, bad
args — return a command with no logger and nothing buffered to lose.
cobra.OnFinalize covers the same paths, but finalizers take no command or
context, so using it would need a package-level holder — the global this
change removes — and it appends to a cobra global with no deregister.
Pinned by TestExecutedCommandCarriesLoggerOnFailure over both leak paths.

The package-level Debug/Info/Warn/Error helpers stay as they are and now
resolve only from the context, falling back to slog.Default(). One
consequence worth knowing: lines logged through context.Background() used

nine such sites are Debug and drop at INFO; opencode.go's ReadSession
warning is the exception, and threading a context there means changing an

73ad9b500eb502c0bf7c086b2640aac67214f7af
fix(trail): write descriptions through the body route, not the metadata PATCH

`entire trail update --body` sent the description as a `body` field on
PATCH /api/v1/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}/{number}. That route does not
serve body writes at all: it rejects the field and names the dedicated
route to use instead. Because the rejection has been served as a redacted
5xx, the caller only ever saw a bare "Service Unavailable" — so this read
as a flaky server, and was measured across payload sizes and retried over
ten minutes before anyone suspected the route was simply wrong.

Route the description to PUT .../{number}/body instead, with
{"markdown": ..., "overwrite": true}. Overwrite is what makes editing an
existing description work: left false the route refuses any non-empty
description with 409 document_not_empty, i.e. every write except the
first. It also matches what --body already means — the interactive path
shows the current description before you edit it. Its If-Match
alternative is not a substitute: that ETag is only handed out by a body
write's own response, so obtaining one means being refused and retrying,
which clobbers exactly as overwrite does a round trip later.

api.TrailUpdateRequest loses its Body field entirely, so sending a
description on the metadata route is no longer representable, and
splitTrailUpdate — which existed only to send the body as its own PATCH —
goes with it. Metadata and description still travel as two non-atomic
requests, and the existing "metadata was updated, but the body update
failed" error is unchanged.

The route and its request shape were verified against the deployed cell's
OpenAPI, not just the server source: PUT
/trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}/{number}/body accepts markdown/contentJson
plus overwrite. No status code is pinned in the CLI's comments or tests —
the rejection has been a redacted 5xx and is moving to a 4xx, and the CLI
must behave the same either way.

Resolve repo-scoped cell targets via processing placement, not mirrors

resolveRepoCellTarget/resolveRepoCellPlacement scanned mirrors and
refused (falling back to home-jurisdiction routing) whenever a repo
was mirrored in more than one region. For a 4-region repo like
entirehq/entire.io this made entire trail/experts silently read the
wrong region's data instead of erroring.

Resolve the repo's PROCESSING placement via the control plane's
consolidated repos index (ListRepos + primaries.processing) instead,
mirroring the entire.io BFF's processingPlacement() selection. Every
resolution failure is now a loud, returned error instead of a silent
nil/fallback — for repo-scoped data a wrong-region "success" is worse
than a command failure.

Also fixes two regressions the fail-loud change introduced in callers
that weren't audited for it: renderDataAPIAuthError was swallowing
`entire trail` commands into total silence on a slow control plane
(it couldn't distinguish the caller's own context firing from the
resolver's internal timeout), and the background trail-enablement
cache could no longer record a definitive "not onboarded" decision,
leaving SessionStart re-forking refresh children indefinitely for
non-onboarded repos.

feat(codex): track subagents via Codex's SubagentStart/SubagentStop hooks

Codex was the one agent named in the original subagent-tracking request with zero
subagent tracking, even though it ships first-class hooks for it. Wire them.

Codex's identity fields are the opposite of what the names suggest, and getting
this backwards would attribute subagent work to a session Entire has never seen:

  - session_id is "the identity shared by the root thread and all descendant
    threads" (session/session.rs) — the *user's* session. It maps straight to
    SessionID.
  - agent_id is the subagent thread's own id. Codex sends no tool_use_id, so
    agent_id doubles as ToolUseID: it is the only value correlating a start with
    its stop, and Entire keys pre-task state (pre-task-<id>.json) and the task
    metadata directory on ToolUseID.

SubagentStop also carries two transcripts — transcript_path is the parent rollout,
agent_transcript_path the subagent's own. Rather than teach the framework a second
layout to guess, add Event.SubagentTranscriptPath so an agent can *declare* where
its subagent transcript is; handleLifecycleSubagentEnd prefers it and falls back to
the Claude Code layout guess. A declared-but-missing path warns rather than
silently substituting, because that disagreement is exactly what went unnoticed
while the guess quietly returned "" for every non-Claude agent.

That mechanism immediately fixes a second agent: Cursor has parsed
agent_transcript_path into its raw struct all along and never forwarded it, so

fix(lifecycle): decide the final-capture eager condense on fresh session phase

handleSubagentStopFinal decided its eager-condense trigger using the
session-state snapshot loaded at the top of the function, before
claimInFlightTask and captureSubagentTaskStep ran. If a racing SessionEnd
flipped the session to PhaseEnded during that capture window (both
serialize on the per-session gate, so the interleaving reduces to
ordering), the stale snapshot still read idle, the eager condense was
skipped, and the just-written task step became post-condensation zombie
shadow data.

Reload session state after captureSubagentTaskStep and decide on the
fresh phase instead. A reload error or a missing state falls back to the
pre-capture phase rather than skipping the decision, since silently
treating a read hiccup as "not ended" would reintroduce the same zombie
class. The initial load remains valid only for the zombie guard (missing
state) and logging.

Adds TestHandleLifecycleSubagentEnd_SubagentStop_SessionEndsMidCapture_StillCondenses,
which uses a callback on the mock analyzer's ExtractModifiedFilesFromOffset
to flip the persisted session to PhaseEnded mid-capture, deterministically
reproducing the race. Verified the test fails against the stale-check
version and passes with the fix.

fix(checkpoint): require the push destination to confirm checkpoint_remote ownership

checkpoint_remote is committed in .entire/settings.json, so cloning or
forking a project inherits it, and a guard exists so a contributor's
session transcripts are not pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint
repo. #1898 keyed that guard on origin's owner, which assumes origin is
yours.

It is not, in one of the two ways to contribute to someone else's project:

  fork first, clone the fork -> origin contributor/app -> mismatch, ignored
  clone the base, add a fork -> origin acme/app        -> MATCHES, honored

In the second the setting reads as ours, and a contributor pushing to
their own fork aims their transcripts at acme/checkpoints. The pre-push
gate cannot catch it because a configured checkpoint_remote is exempt
from the gate by design, so a wrong ownership verdict goes straight
through.

Ownership now requires every remote that identifies the repo to be owned
by the checkpoint repo's owner: origin says which project this is, the
push destination says which repo we are writing to. One mismatch means
inherited. The settings.local.json provenance short-circuit and the
no-origin fallback are unchanged.

The trade: a repo of our own with a differently-owned secondary remote no
longer routes checkpoints to our checkpoint repo on pushes to that
remote. The two topologies are indistinguishable from local git config —
both are origin=<owner>/app plus a push destination owned by somebody
else — so one of them has to lose. Pushes to the elected sync remote are
unaffected, ENT-1451's gate already blocks checkpoint sync on pushes to a
non-elected remote, and erring toward "not ours" never writes transcripts
to a repository we cannot confirm we own. On git-refs it strictly helps:
the push queue records only a ref, so a delivery to the wrong destination
drains the queue and the checkpoint never reaches the right repo at all.

Not addressed: FetchURL applies no ownership check, so a repo whose
writes were diverted still reads from the configured checkpoint repo.
Pre-existing, affects both fork topologies, wants its own change.

fix(checkpoint): persist a captured sync remote only after delivery

Capture wrote the election as soon as it decided a push qualified, before
the push ran. Between that decision and the network there are five ways
delivery still does not happen: a diverged checkpoint policy, an OPF
decision failure or user abort, an OPF rewrite failure, the empty-remote
defer, and a rejected transfer. On any of them the pre-push announced
"Checkpoints now sync to X" and moved the election permanently while X
received nothing.

The permanence is what makes it more than a cosmetic lie. The election is
one-shot ("first capture sticks"), so afterwards the still-queued
checkpoints could only drain to the remote that had just failed to take
them, and the user's route out was to hand-edit
strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote or delete the state file.

The most likely way to hit it needs no failure at all: add a fresh empty
fork, push your branch to it for the first time. That push declares the
fork, so capture fired — and it is exactly the push the empty-remote defer
suppresses, because publishing entire/checkpoints/v1 to a remote with no
branches lets a forge adopt it as the default branch.

Capture is now two-phase, straddling prePush:

  pendingCaptureCheckpointSyncRemote  decide, write nothing
  <the existing gate, policy, OPF and push>
  commitCapturedSyncRemote            persist + announce

The gate takes the pending remote as a second argument, because the push
that elects a remote has to be allowed to carry the checkpoints that
justify the election. Both backends commit at their own success point: the
git-branch path after the ref-push loop, the git-refs path when the queue
flush returns no error. An empty queue commits too — nothing was stranded,
so following the push is safe either way.

The lock covers each phase separately rather than spanning the push, which
would serialize unrelated worktrees on a network operation. commit
therefore re-checks eligibility under the lock, so two hooks that reach the
same pending answer resolve to whoever's state lands first; "first capture
sticks" is now decided at the write, not at the proposal.

reproduces the fresh-fork case (captured "fork", status "observed", zero
checkpoints delivered) and then confirms the following push both delivers

silently, since an untrusted hook simply never fires. Mirroring a clamp we

8581735744a91586c16517a499ead6e1b3951814
refactor(strategy): converge identity linking on proclive, delete proctree

Trail review (1061) found internal/proctree duplicating the existing
proclive package: same ancestry walk, same per-platform introspection
(one sysctl/stat parse apart), and — decisively — proclive's Identity is
already persisted on EVERY turn start as SessionState.Owner by
captureSessionOwner, seven lines from where this branch re-walked the
same process tree into a second field. The review also showed the
duplicate's Windows walker ran in no CI job (the Windows job filters on
test names carrying Windows/MSYS; none did), had an orphan-reparenting
hazard PID recycling makes real, cost one process-table snapshot per
ancestry level, and that the shell filter was missing "entire" and "go"
— both already on proclive's transient list.

Converge instead of duplicating:

- proclive gains HasAncestor(Identity) — the commit-attribution
  question ("was this process spawned, however indirectly, by the
  recorded owner?") with proclive's host, boot, and start-fingerprint
  guards, so a recycled PID or an identity recorded on another machine
  can never match — two guards the deleted package lacked (its own doc
  conceded the Linux cross-reboot collision that proclive's bootID
  closes). Plus IdentityOf(pid) for callers and tests.
- findSessionByCommitAncestry matches SessionState.Owner via
  HasAncestor. No new recording, no AgentAncestry field, no
  refreshAgentAncestry (Owner is re-captured every turn start, which
  already covers resume under a new agent process). Ties — one agent
  process hosting several sessions, or a nested agent whose outer agent
  is also an ancestor — go to the most recently interacting session.
- internal/proctree is deleted. On platforms proclive cannot introspect
  (Windows), identity matching reports nothing and linking falls back
  to worktree matching — honestly, rather than via platform code no CI
  job executed.

This also positions PR #1777 (cross-common-dir auto-adopt): its
owner-matching compares first-non-transient identities and breaks when
a non-transient wrapper interposes at commit time; HasAncestor's
any-ancestor semantics are immune and reusable there.

11773e1e37f2411ee096f4e72cda55d3c12b6e4c
fix(checkpoint): address review findings on the read-remotes chain

High severity:

- Attach's local-presence gates are local-only again. The read chain
  selects per checkpoint across local and remote-tracking trees, so a
  stale-but-existing local v1 branch fell through to origin's tracking
  tree and reported a checkpoint "present" that the next local write
  would not build on — the exact clobber the gate exists to prevent
  ("Only local presence counts"). New PersistentRefs.PrimaryAsLocalRead
  pins reads to the local ref with no remote tiers; both attach guards
  use it. The main attach store meanwhile gains the read chain it was
  missing, so informational reads reach the elected remote.

- Checkpoint-ref hydration no longer installs a legacy tip under
  elected-remote uncertainty. FetchCheckpointRefFrom installs the
  canonical LOCAL ref (+ref:ref); checkpoint refs advance (backfills
  parent onto the tip); and hydration only runs when the ref is absent
  locally — so falling through to origin while the elected remote (the
  only remote writes confine to) was merely unreachable permanently
  installed a possibly-stale tip. The chain now advances only on
  authoritative absence; transport failure aborts. The git-branch
  read path is unchanged (pure tree reads install nothing), and the
  integration matrix now pins the split per backend.

- A FAILED election with a missing local primary seeds from origin's
  real history instead of a fresh orphan. Checkpoint pushes are already
  fail-closed while the election is broken, so the orphan bought no
  safety — but it guaranteed a disjoint history (non-fast-forward on
  every sync) the moment the user fixed checkpoint_push_remote. Seeding
  a MISSING ref is not the #1374 replay-on-divergence hazard; the
  elected-exists confinement pin is unchanged.

Medium severity:

- agentimport's idempotency listing consults the read chain
  (Options.ReadRemotes, wired by both callers): turns already on the
  elected remote were re-imported, turns only in origin's stale
  tracking ref were wrongly skipped.
- GetCheckpointAuthor iterates the same chain as content reads, so
  explain no longer shows an empty author for checkpoints whose commit
  lives only on a remote tier.
- checkpointpolicy.SyncFrom reports the ENFORCED (local) policy when a
  read-only legacy baseline could not advance the local ref, instead of
  printing a policy the hooks never enforce; the unadopted baseline
  stays visible via RemoteHash.
- The resume metadata fetch skips already-present legacy tracking refs
  after a successful elected fetch (bootstrap-only), halving steady-
  state deep fetches; a fresh clone still bootstraps origin's legacy
  tier once.
- resolveSessionsBranchTrees skips candidates whose commit is an
  ancestor of an already-kept tree, eliminating the duplicate shard
  walk when the local branch is ahead of a tracking ref.

Deferred with rationale: making OpenOptions.ReadRemotes self-derivable
inside checkpoint.Open (finding: hand-threading at ~15 sites) requires
checkpoint to import strategy — an import cycle. The explicit wiring
plus the attach fix above is the practical mitigation; revisit if the
chain resolver ever moves below the checkpoint package.

fix(checkpoint): never memoize a failed remote read

Review findings against the per-invocation remote cache added earlier in this PR.

Sticky wrong answers. Both underlying reads erased failure into a legitimate
value: readRemotesInConfigOrder returned nil for any `git config --get-regexp`
error, and isConfiguredRemote returned false for any `git remote get-url` error.
That was harmless while every call re-ran the command, but the cache memoized
those as real answers — so one fork failure under load, one cancelled context or
one locked .git/config made the election answer "this repo has no remotes" for the
rest of the process, and checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote then skipped checkpoint
sync silently. The mirror image was worse: a memoized false made
ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote fail closed on a configured checkpoint_push_remote
("is not a configured git remote") until the command exited.

Both reads now report failure separately from their answer, discriminating on the
process actually having run: `git config --get-regexp` exits 1 for no match, so
that exit code alone is the empty answer, and a `git remote get-url` that exited
non-zero really did say "no such remote" while one that could not start says
nothing about it. The cache stores successes only; a failure answers the current
call and leaves the slot unset so the next one retries.
TestGitRemoteCache_FailedReadsAreNotMemoized pins both directions.

Inverted locking comment. snapshotFor's doc claimed "Callers hold c.mu" while the
function acquires it — a leftover from moving the lock in 0a833207f. A caller who
believed it would self-deadlock on the non-reentrant mutex, hanging every command,
and the surrounding two-level-locking commentary makes it credible.

Tests depended on the test process's cwd. The memoization assertions installed the
cache on a bare context, so gitReadRepo fell back to resolving the repo from cwd
and nothing cached at all outside a git worktree — three assertions would fail for
reasons unrelated to the cache. They now pin the repository with
settings.WithWorktreeRoot, as the partition tests already did.

Invalidation skipped a completed mutation. applyMirrorRemotePlan invalidated only
on its success path, so a failure in the second git write left the first — a real
`git remote add` — uninvalidated. Now deferred across both writes.

Misleading timeout diagnostic. fetchMetadataFromRemote reported a hardcoded "2
minutes" for any DeadlineExceeded, but a later candidate is bounded by what the
chain ceiling has left, often about one. It now takes the tighter of its own window
and the remaining chain budget, and names that.

matching main.

f86f8a42c541d9ee760bc3e27105168dafe534e1
feat(strategy): link commits to sessions by process identity

Commit-to-session linking guessed by worktree path: the commit hooks
matched SessionState.WorktreePath against the commit's worktree. Any
drift between that bookkeeping and reality lost the linkage — an agent
committing in a sibling worktree produced an unlinked commit, or worse:
with a poisoned state dir, a wrong link. Both happened for real (three
retro-attach incidents; most recently a leaked test fixture session,
sessC, was linked to a commit and stamped a dangling trailer whose
checkpoint was never written).

Identity-first linking removes the guessing for agent commits. At
session start the hook records its nearest process ancestors
(pid + start time; the agent process is among them, since agents run
hooks as children) in SessionState.AgentAncestry. At commit time the
hook walks its own ancestry (git <- tool shell <- agent) and matches
those refs: nearest ancestor wins, ties go to the most recently
interacting session, start times guard against PID reuse. The identity
match is UNIONED with the worktree-matched set, never a replacement —
a commit condenses every session with pending content in its worktree,
and identity adds the one that path matching missed.

A commit identity-matched outside the session's home worktree is
guest-linked: condensed and linked, but worktree-coupled state
(BaseCommit, shadow-branch realignment) is never mutated from a foreign
worktree — shadow branches are keyed by BaseCommit + WorktreeID, and
the session's next home commit must still match.

The worktree fallback (human commits, severed process trees) is
hardened in the same pass:

- Imported sessions never link: they are historical records, and a
  leaked imported fixture is exactly what hijacked the sessC commit.
- Multi-worktree ambiguity is filtered to sessions that interacted
  within the last 15 minutes; a single live worktree links, two live
  worktrees still decline — now with a stderr hint naming
  'entire session adopt' instead of only a log-level warning.

And the leak that poisoned the state dir is closed at both ends:
agent import scopes its session-state store to the repo being imported
into (new session.NewStateStoreForWorktree) instead of the process CWD,
and under 'go test' the CWD-resolved store refuses to open outside the
temp root, so any future non-isolated test fails loudly instead of
writing fixtures into a developer's real .git/entire-sessions. The full
unit suite passes with the guard on — the agentimport tests were the
only leakers.

New internal/proctree package: cross-platform process ancestry
(darwin sysctl, linux /proc, windows toolhelp) with pid+starttime
identity.

fix(checkpoint): never splice a single-JSON-value transcript

The prefix cache gated on filename plus size, which is not sufficient to
establish that splicing is sound. OpenCode's transcript is a single JSON object
({"info":...,"messages":[...]}) and lifecycle.go writes it to the very same
paths.TranscriptFileName path other agents write JSONL to, newline-terminated
because the export's stdout is redirected straight to the file. So it satisfied
every guard.

Once such a file passed 1MiB, a later checkpoint would reuse the prefix and redact
only the appended bytes -- but a fragment of a single JSON value does not parse,
so RedactBlobBytes drops out of the field-aware whole-document pass into raw regex
and entropy detection over partial JSON. That is precisely the identifier
corruption and under-redaction redactSingleJSONValue exists to prevent, applied
silently to part of a committed and pushed transcript.

The invariant the cache rests on -- redact(A+B) == redact(A)+redact(B) -- holds
only for line-delimited content, so gate on that directly rather than inferring it
from a filename: redact.IsLineDelimited reports whether JSONLContent will take the
per-line path, and its tests pin it to mirror the redactor's own routing decision.

Both gates are kept, because they establish different things: the filename
establishes append-only (transcript.jsonl is regenerated, full.jsonl.001 chunks are
not appended), and IsLineDelimited establishes composability.

perf(checkpoint): reuse the redacted transcript prefix across checkpoints

full.jsonl holds the full session and is appended to, but every checkpoint

appended. Two properties make the splice sound:

  - Redaction is per-line and stateless, so redact(A+B) == redact(A)+redact(B).

    what depends on it.
  - A stored prefix always ends immediately after a newline, so the redacted
    prefix does too and plain byte concatenation reproduces the full result with

matches, so a rewritten or compacted transcript, changed custom rules, or a CLI
upgrade all fall back to redacting everything. The fingerprint mixes the CLI

vendored ruleset, which is not introspectable: an upgrade costs one full redaction.

A caller that caches redacted bytes needs to know when the bytes were produced
under different rules. Hash the inputs that change the eight regex layers' output:
the custom-rule set (inline plus rule packs, sorted so map order cannot leak into
the hash) and the PII layer's enablement, per-category toggles, and user patterns.

configFingerprintVersion is mixed in and MUST be bumped whenever the layers change
behaviour in a way the hashed config cannot see -- a new layer, an altered
pattern, a different placeholder token, or a change to how regions are merged.
That makes it part of the pipeline's contract, not an implementation detail.

Two things it deliberately cannot cover, documented on the function: the OpenAI
Privacy Filter, whose output is not a pure function of local config, so cached
bytes must never be shared between OPF and non-OPF paths; and the betterleaks
ruleset version, which the library does not expose, so a caller that caches across
upgrades has to mix in the binary's own version.

1ac6a1e37e1fc8ed67cb05320260f6bf8006a3f8
perf(redact): shard JSONL line redaction across goroutines

Redaction is the dominant cost of storing a large transcript: profiling the
checkpoint blob write put it at ~99.7% of the total (git object writing was
174ms of a 66.7s pass on 70MB), and 82% of that is betterleaks' regex ruleset
under Go's NFA engine.

Every line is redacted in isolation by a stateless redactor, so the line pass can
be split. Shard it and rejoin in order; output is byte-identical.

Shards are sized by bytes rather than one-per-core, for two reasons. Per-byte cost
climbs with input size (allocation and GC pressure over one large buffer), so
small pieces are cheaper per byte *and* run concurrently -- measured on a 20MB
Codex transcript, 43s sequential vs 2.1s across 12 shards, which is superlinear in
shard count and not explainable by parallelism alone. And balancing by bytes
rather than line count matters because agent transcripts mix thousands of short
lines with occasional multi-MB tool results, where equal line counts would leave
one oversized shard as the tail.

Sharding is gated on an explicit argument describing the redactor, not on which
entry point the caller reached. String is pure and opts in; the OPF flow's
collector closures accumulate into a shared map and slice and opt out. Stating it
per call site is what lets batch.go's OPF-disabled fast path -- the same pure
String redactor over whole transcript blobs -- take the win too.

Also preallocates the line builder from the input size (4.5x on a 1MiB shard,
which helps the sequential path as well).

Verified safe to share the layer config across goroutines: the betterleaks
Detect path does not mutate the shared detector (all mutation is confined to
Run), and the custom-rule, PII, and detector globals are sync.Once/RWMutex
guarded. Tests assert sharded output equals sequential across a fixture that
exercises every layer, plus shard boundaries, edge shapes, and the
redact(A+B) == redact(A)+redact(B) property that callers splitting a transcript
depend on. Passes -race.

0a833207fa94de3d912f6589785913e51647f314
perf(checkpoint): stop the remote cache serializing cross-repository git reads

The cache held its single mutex across the git subprocess, not just the map
access. `entire dispatch --repos a,b` fans out over repositories with an errgroup
(dispatch/mode_local.go:109), so every repository's git read queued behind every
other's — serializing work that ran concurrently before this cache existed. The
per-repository partitioning added in f6770e793 gave each repo its own entry but
they all still contended on one lock.

Locking is now two-level: gitRemoteCache.mu guards only the byDir map and is
never held across an exec, and each repository's answers sit behind their own
mutex. Within one repository callers still serialize, which is the point for two
racing reads of the same key — the second waits and takes the memoized answer
instead of shelling out again. Two reads of different keys in one repository
serialize too; the key set is tiny (the remote list, plus membership for the
elected remote and origin), so that is a bounded cost for a much simpler
invariant than per-key locking.

Invalidation still just drops the map: a goroutine already holding a snapshot
finishes against it and its result is discarded with the old map rather than being
observed after the mutation.

TestGitRemoteCache_CrossRepoReadsDoNotSerialize pins it, ordered so the outcome
cannot depend on which goroutine starts first — A enters its read, and only then
is B allowed to call. Verified to fail (10s deadline) with the lock held across
the read and pass without.

4f1c1a324b0c9c30e3265276aa09ce4b32ff3f2f
refactor(logging): attach the session ID without re-initializing

The hook path called Init a second time once it had resolved the session ID.
The log path is fixed — Init's own doc said the session ID is "used only for
the slog attribute, not the filename" — so that second call closed and reopened
the same file, discarded and reallocated the 8KB buffer, and re-read the log
level, all to add one attribute. On every hook invocation.

It was also the only thing in a live process that re-initialized, which is what
made a logger captured beforehand able to end up writing into an orphaned
buffer. Removing it removes that failure mode; liveWriter stays for the
exclusive write lock, which fixed a real race.

Attaching a session is a fact about a logger, not a reason to rebuild the sink,
so it now follows the shape this package already uses for such facts:
WithSessionID(ctx, id), next to WithComponent and WithAgent. Init drops its
sessionID parameter and does one thing — open the sink.

WithSessionID stamps the logger rather than storing a context value, unlike its
two neighbours: redact holds the injected logger directly and would otherwise
lose session_id from exactly the diagnostics where it matters most. It owns the
ID validation that used to live in Init, and a rejected ID no longer aborts the
hook path — which previously skipped configuring redaction entirely because a
malformed session ID made Init return an error.

refactor(logging): return the logger from Init instead of a context

Init both opened the sink and decided where the handle lived, returning a
context.Context. In Go, ctx is an input — the only functions that return one
are explicit WithX(ctx, v) decorators — so an initializer handing one back
conflates process lifecycle with request-scoped value propagation, hides from
the signature that anything was injected, and forced `ctx = logCtx` at every
call site.

Init now returns the initialized logger (session_id already stamped, since
that is part of initializing it) and each caller injects with WithLogger. The
one exported context decorator does the context work; contextWithInitLogger,
which existed only to bridge the two, is gone.

This also moves a status signal out of the context and into the return type: a
nil logger with a nil error now says "initialized, but not file-backed"
explicitly, where before callers had to infer the stderr fallback from an
invisible absence in the context. It cannot be an error — the hook path must
still configure redaction when logging falls back — hence the documented
nilnil exemption.

f6770e79330fe7c3ea929cfe8e484a6db96b5ed4
fix(checkpoint): partition the remote cache per repository, and finish the chain

Addresses the three open findings on this trail.

Cross-repo staleness (high). The remote-read cache was keyed only by remote name
and a single ordered slice, with no repository scoping, while `entire dispatch
--repos a,b` walks several repositories in ONE process — scoping each election
with settings.WithWorktreeRoot so the git calls run in that repo
(dispatch/mode_local.go, whose own comment says so). Repo B's election would have
answered from repo A's remote list, silently re-breaking c04a2e312 ("honor read
candidates per repository"). Answers are now partitioned by repository root:
the context's scoped worktree root when there is one, else the repo containing
the process working directory that git would inherit. The repo root rather than
the raw cwd because `git remote get-url` answers the same from any subdirectory,
so subdirectory calls should share one entry; paths.WorktreeRoot is memoized per
cwd, so the partition costs far less than the subprocess it protects. An
unidentifiable repository disables caching for that call rather than sharing
another's answers. Pinned by TestGitRemoteCache_PartitionsByRepository.

Doc claimed more than the code did. The cache's comment stated that long-lived
commands — naming `dispatch` and `runner --run` alongside `mcp` — "must scope
their own window", but only mcp does. With per-repository partitioning the
multi-repo correctness problem is structural rather than each caller's to
remember, so the comment now says what is actually true: partitioning handles
repository identity, per-request windows handle freshness over time, and mcp is
the one command that needs the latter today.

RestoreLogsOnly missed the read chain. It was the one checkpoint.Open call site
in this branch still opening without ReadRemotes, so `entire session resume`'s
logs-only path fell back to the legacy origin-only tier and could fail to find
metadata that resume/explain now read from a non-origin elected remote.

Election cost is unchanged by the partition: `entire checkpoint list` still spends
9 git subprocesses, matching main.

c32e8f23055d2864e540260bd76f1332cc252179
perf(checkpoint): bound the read chain and stop re-electing per call

Fixes two costs this PR's read-candidate chain introduced, both measured
against origin/main with a PATH-shimmed git counting subprocesses.

Unbounded worst case. Per-candidate budgets replaced single shared ones —
a real fix, since one shared budget let a hung leader starve the legacy
origin tier — but nothing bounded the total, and these read paths have no
outer deadline: `entire resume` sets none and main() uses
context.WithCancel, not WithTimeout. fetchBlobsByHash lost the most: it
used to run inside one 2-minute budget that also covered its fallback
fetches, and per-target budgets left those fallbacks on the caller's
uncapped context, so a stalled hydration could spend per-target budgets
and then a fresh per-candidate metadata chain on top.

ReadChainBudget now wraps all three chains — checkpoint ref hydration, the
metadata branch chain, and blob hydration including its fallbacks — with
per-candidate budgets nested inside, so every candidate keeps its own
window while the total stays bounded.

Sized as an absolute 3 minutes rather than "n tiers x one full window".
The multiple is the trap: at 2 x ReadFetchTimeout with today's two tiers
the ceiling equals the loop's own worst case, so it cannot bind and buys
nothing, and blob hydration's fallbacks inherit an already-expired
context. An absolute ceiling binds for every chain of two or more
candidates, leaves a single-candidate chain untouched, and does not go
quietly wrong when a third tier appears. ReadChainLoopBudget holds back a
sixth of it so the fallbacks are funded rather than merely inside it, and
ReadFetchTimeout is exported so the cli-side paths stop carrying their own
2-minute literals that had to stay silently equal to it.

Election cost per command. The election re-runs on every call by design,
and each run shells out to git twice over .git/config: which remotes
exist, and does remote X exist. One command elects several times —
`entire checkpoint list` resolves the chain four times (disconnection
warning, branch listing, the git-refs store's remote discovery, imported
rewind points), spending 15 git subprocesses where main spent 9.

WithGitRemoteCache memoizes only those two .git/config reads, installed on
the root context in main(). The election result, settings, and the
captured-election file stay uncached, so a write followed by a re-resolve
still sees the new value — #1991's capture keeps working, which caching the
election result would have silently broken. Context-scoped and opt-in, so
an uninstrumented context behaves exactly as before and tests cannot leak
one temp repo's remote list into another.

Process scope is not invocation scope for every command: `entire mcp`
serves an agent session from one context, so it installs a fresh cache per
request via WithFreshGitRemoteCache rather than pinning one snapshot of
"which remotes exist" for hours. `entire repo mirror use` is the only
git-remote mutation in the CLI and invalidates after its writes.

WarnIfMetadataDisconnected now takes the caller's context instead of
building context.Background(): the detached context ignored both interrupt
cancellation and the cache, re-shelling out for answers the caller already
had.

Measured, `entire checkpoint list`: main 9 subprocesses, this PR before
these changes 15, after 9 — the regression is fully recovered (1 config
--get-regexp and 2 remote get-url, same as main).

Tests: the ceiling test stalls every target under a production-shaped
ratio (ceiling below targets x per-target, which is what makes it bind)
and asserts the call returns in ~ceiling — 0.58s with the ceiling, 1.09s
and failing without. Cache tests cover opt-in behavior, empty lists as
real answers, negative caching, invalidation, and an end-to-end guard that
a remote added mid-invocation is visible to a later election after
invalidation.

2661867ad980f4f63d44ab9cefe98bef57688ec4
feat(strategy): capture the checkpoint sync remote from tracked pushes

The single-remote election (ENT-1451) guesses the sync destination from
config at rest — origin, else sole, else first in .git/config — so a user
whose branches push a non-origin remote had checkpoints strand locally
until they hand-configured checkpoint_push_remote. First user report
landed the day after v0.10.0 shipped.

Capture makes the election follow demonstrated push behavior with zero
configuration: during pre-push, a push whose target agrees with the
branch's declared push destination (branch.<name>.pushRemote ->
remote.pushDefault -> branch.<name>.remote — the config a bare
'git push' resolves through) and differs from the current election
persists that remote as the captured election, announces it on stderr,
and the same push carries the checkpoints. The captured tier sits
between the explicit setting and origin, and is fail-soft: a captured
remote that was renamed or removed falls through to the default tiers
instead of disabling sync.

Neither signal elects alone. Declaration without a push is the
config-at-rest bug that got the static tracking tier dropped (74e239a9:
a 'clone -o base' stranded every origin push); a push without
declaration is the pre-single-remote transcript leak (a one-off
'git push upstream' must never publish transcripts). Capture acts only
on their intersection.

Phase-1 rules: at most one captured remote and the first capture sticks,
so a mixed-habit repo whose branches push two remotes cannot flip the
election on every push. The state file is list-shaped from day one so
the multi-remote set (per-remote push-queue tracking) needs no
migration. An explicit checkpoint_push_remote outranks and disables
capture.

The existing single-remote integration tests set up their gated remote
with 'push -u', which under capture is a declared destination — their
setups now reset tracking so they keep pinning the undeclared-one-off
shape, and TestCheckpointSyncRemote_BranchTrackingDoesNotReroute is
split into its two surviving truths: tracking alone still never reroutes
(the 74e239a9 regression pin), and a tracked push now legitimately
captures.

Merge note: reads still resolve through origin until the read-side stack
(#1956/#1951) lands; this PR must merge after it so captured non-origin
elections are readable end to end.

976fd426117035ece6ba13f102814e447ddcd5c6
fix(login): open the browser via ShellExecute on Windows

`entire login` on Windows opened
https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli and the
authorization server rejected it with "auth request is missing redirect
uri" (reported against v0.10.0).

openBrowser launched `cmd /c start "" <url>`, and cmd.exe treats an
unquoted `&` as a command separator, so the browser only ever received
the text before the first `&`. Go's argv escaping does not help:
syscall.EscapeArg only quotes an argument containing a space, tab,
quote, or backslash, and a URL has none of those, so it reached cmd.exe
bare. Because url.Values.Encode sorts keys, client_id sorts first and
redirect_uri sits behind three separators — hence the exact URL in the
report. Quoting alone would not be enough either: the percent-encoded
redirect_uri also exposes the URL to cmd's `%VAR%` expansion.

Split the launcher per platform and, on Windows, call ShellExecute
directly (as github.com/pkg/browser does) so the URL is passed as a
single wide string with no command line to parse. golang.org/x/sys was
already a direct dependency. macOS/Linux keep exec'ing open/xdg-open,
which never involved a shell.

Only the default browser redirect was affected. `entire login --device`
was a working workaround because its verification_uri_complete carries a
single query parameter, so it survives cmd.exe intact.

Tests run in the existing test-windows CI job (it selects `-run
'(Windows|MSYS)'`): one asserts the whole URL reaches the shell
association, and one executes `cmd /c echo <url>` to pin the truncation
as the root cause so the shell launcher is not reintroduced.

Not addressed here: runBrowserLogin only prints the full URL when the
browser open reports failure, so this mangled-but-"successful" launch
left the user no copy-paste fallback.

1d36ecb67d703cb6f97d0450d7c58182dde4c4ed
fix: address review of the codex session-end work

Four fixes from the bot review on #1940, plus the e2e gap the first one led
to.

AreHooksInstalled required every event in managedHooks, so adding SessionEnd
un-installed Codex for everyone who enabled it before this release. Worse than
it sounds: DetectPresence delegates to it, so such a repo was neither installed
nor detected — Codex vanished from `entire status`, the review and investigate
pickers, and a non-interactive `entire enable` re-run (which keeps the
currently installed agents) would have dropped it rather than repaired it. Only
the four pre-existing events gate the check now; the missing hook is drift,
which MissingEntireHooks already reports with `entire enable` as the fix, and
setupAgentHooks installs unconditionally so that fix still works.

That in turn exposed a hole in e2e. The suite pre-trusts hooks by recomputing
Codex's trusted_hash values itself, from a hand-maintained event table that did
not know SessionEnd — and Codex silently skips hooks with no trust entry. The
hook would have been installed but inert for every e2e run, with nothing
failing to say so. The table learns SessionEnd, and a new test installs hooks
for real and requires a trust entry per Entire handler, so the two can't drift
again.

logging.Close left the logger in place while closing the buffer underneath it.
The handler holds that *bufio.Writer by value, so anything logged after the
sweep's cleanup went into an orphaned buffer over a closed file and was never
flushed — `entire doctor` keeps condensing and discarding sessions after the
sweep returns. Close now drops the logger too. On its own that would push those
lines back onto the terminal, which fe46a7333 set out to prevent, so
finalizeExitedSessions returns its cleanup instead of deferring it internally
and doctor scopes it to the whole command.

status filtered active sessions on EndedAt while `session stop` filtered on
IsEnded. Not just legacy state: `entire session attach` sets Phase to ended
without stamping EndedAt, so an attached session showed as active in status and
`session stop` then refused to list it. All three status sites use IsEnded, which
makes the comment on filterActiveSessions true rather than merely reworded.

c22c538384e9b92fd07385b8f83aa1815d775946
fix(hooks): bound the agent-hook status walk so pathological repos degrade instead of hanging

go-git's Worktree.Status walks the whole worktree and is not
context-cancellable. On a pathological repo (live incident: a stray
`git init` in $HOME with no .gitignore) the walk ground for hours in
hook processes that outlived the agent's ~60s hook timeout — two
zombies at ~1.8GB RSS, one with 25 CPU-minutes — while the failure
stayed completely silent: no session state, no checkpoint, no log line.

Add gitrepo.StatusWithBudget: a 20s wall-clock budget (headroom under
the agent timeout for the rest of the capture path) enforced by a
goroutine+select wrapper that abandons the walk on breach — the
orphaned goroutine dies with the one-shot hook process, which is the
point. On breach it returns an error wrapping
gitrepo.ErrStatusBudgetExceeded, emits an actionable Warn naming the
repo root, elapsed, budget, and consequence, and latches a
process-local flag so no later walk in the same hook process re-enters
the worktree (the turn-start hook walks twice: pre-prompt capture and
prompt attribution).

Route the agent-hook call sites through it — DetectFileChanges
(turn-end, subagent-end, PostTodo), the pre-prompt/pre-task untracked
scans, and the prompt-attribution walk — and make the pre-prompt/
pre-task captures fail open on status errors instead of failing the
hook: capture proceeds with transcript-derived data, and a new
UntrackedScanSkipped marker tells the paired end-hook to skip new-file
detection so pre-existing untracked files are not misattributed to the
agent. Git-hook paths (post-commit condensation) never call Status;
review/rewind keep the unbounded Status since a user is actively
waiting there.

feat(codex): finalize sessions via Codex's SessionEnd hook

Codex gained a SessionEnd hook in 0.146 (openai/codex#33895, "Add SessionEnd
hooks for thread teardown"). Until now Entire only registered SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, Stop and PostToolUse, so quitting Codex left the session
un-finalized and it showed up in `entire status` indefinitely.

Register it, parse it into the normalized SessionEnd event, and include it in
install/uninstall/detection. The payload is thinner than Codex's other hooks —
no model, permission_mode or turn_id — and its `reason` is a constant, so only
session_id, cwd and transcript_path are consumed.

The hook is subject to a ceiling the others are not: Codex defaults SessionEnd
handlers to 1s and clamps them to 3s (SESSION_END_MAX_TIMEOUT_SEC), warning at
every startup when a config asks for more, then terminates the hook's process
tree on expiry. So hook timeouts become per-event — SessionEnd at exactly the
ceiling, everything else unchanged at 30s — and the command match now includes
the timeout so a hook installed by an older Entire is rewritten rather than
left to nag.

Agents in that position declare a budget through the new optional
SessionEndBudgeter interface, which bounds only the eager condense.
Mark-ended stays unbounded: it is one atomic state-file rename and must always
complete. The bound is best-effort — condensation does not poll ctx between
stages — and exists to stop short of the process-tree kill, not to make
condensation interruptible. Either way of being cut off is safe, since
MutateSessionState persists at the end and PostCommit retries.

fix(session): reclaim IDLE sessions whose agent process exited

State.OwnerExited gated on Phase.IsActive(), which is only PhaseActive. An
agent that finishes its last turn transitions ACTIVE -> IDLE, so a session
whose agent then quit without firing a session-end hook was invisible to the
dead-owner sweep in `entire status` and `entire doctor`.

That is exactly the shape Codex leaves behind — it had no SessionEnd hook
before 0.146 — and it can happen to any agent that is killed before its hook
runs. Those sessions lingered as "active" for 7 days until StaleSessionThreshold
made StateStore.Load delete the state file outright, discarding pending
checkpoint work rather than condensing it.

Process death is unambiguous and phase-independent, so OwnerExited now excludes
only already-finalized sessions (PhaseEnded or EndedAt set). doctor's
classifySession checks it ahead of the phase switch for the same reason; the
repeated stuckSession literals collapse into a local constructor.

shadow-branch rows and sorts the two together by date.

resume view of the current branch, and a row is either a live checkpoint

test(checkpoint): pin the shadow-branch worktree hash to known-answer vectors

HashWorktreeID names half of every shadow branch, and shadow branches are how a
running session finds its own pending checkpoints between invocations. Change
the derivation and an upgraded CLI computes a different branch name for the same
worktree: the in-flight checkpoints are still on disk, nothing looks for them
again, and intra-session rewind quietly loses its history.

Nothing in the repo could see such a change. TestHashWorktreeID asserted only
length, determinism, and that different inputs differ; TestShadowBranchNameForCommit
built its `want` by calling HashWorktreeID — the function under test — so the
hashed half of the name compared against itself. The integration suite is no
backstop either: its shadow-branch assertions go through
env.GetShadowBranchNameForCommit, which calls checkpoint.ShadowBranchNameForCommit.

Mutating the preimage to sha256("wt:" + worktreeID) compiles, keeps all three
properties true, and left ./cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/... green (675 tests).

Replace the derived expectations with literals. The same mutation now fails
three subtests of TestShadowBranchNameForCommit. The length check is kept and
now reads WorktreeIDHashLength rather than a repeated 6.

Only re-mode directories Entire chose to own

Review follow-up to 4ca20d99c, on three points.

EnsurePrivateDir documented that only group and other bits are cleared,
but chmod-ed a flat 0700. An already-private directory returned early, so
a plain 0500 did survive, but a mode both loose and stricter than 0700 in
the owner triad did not: 0555 became 0700. Mask the bits off rather than
replace the mode. Masking can leave the owner no access at all, which is
what an already-private 0000 directory has always gotten from the early
return: this makes a directory private, it does not make it usable.

The token store called EnsurePrivateDir on filepath.Dir of its file, so an
ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH pointing anywhere re-moded whatever directory the
file already lived in. Pointed at $HOME, it silently stripped the group
and other bits; pointed at a CI secret mount or a read-only volume the
caller does not own, the chmod failed and took every Get/Set/Delete with
it. Tighten only a directory Entire picked itself. A user-named one is
still created 0700 when missing, since that directory is new and nothing
else was using it, but an existing one keeps the mode the user gave it.

contexts.FilePath promised "0700 perms", which the preserve-stricter
behaviour never guaranteed.

os.MkdirAll is a no-op on a path that already exists, so the directory's
mode belongs to whichever caller created it first. Three callers create
this one. Two ask for 0700; the third asked for 0755, and because it runs
from the root command's PersistentPostRun it fires after essentially any
command, so on a fresh machine it is almost always the one that wins. The
two 0700 callers could never repair the result.

and clears group and other bits from a directory that already exists.

correcting the creation mode alone would only help users who have not yet
run the CLI. A mode stricter than 0700 is left as the user set it, and
the tightening is skipped on Windows, where the permission bits are
synthetic and Chmod only toggles the read-only flag.

Files in the directory were already written 0600 and are unchanged. What
the loose directory mode granted was traversal and enumeration.

performing the fetch, suggesting `mu.Lock(); defer mu.Unlock(); if

times out after 40s. `defer mu.Unlock()` holds the mutex across the
whole closure body, and the memo write further down re-acquires the same

it were reached the cost is one duplicate fetch, not a wrong answer,
since the memo is an optimization and not a correctness invariant.

than an unreachable duplicate-fetch window justifies.

apply the deadlocking version.

one store and continuing past each failure, paid WriteProbeFetchBudget
(15s) per checkpoint — and FetchingTree.File fetches one hash at a time,
so a read touching several missing blobs paid it several times over.

real ceiling is the agent killing the hook (~60s for Claude Code), after
which nothing past the loop runs.

created the timeout can tell that apart from a caller deadline or a

like `checkpoint explain`, which have a 3-minute budget and a user
watching.

error is cheap to retry and may be one blob's genuine remote absence,
which must not stop the next blob from being fetched. As in the ref

Probe missing checkpoint blobs in one cat-file, not one per blob

collectMissingBlobs asked git about every storer miss individually, so a
checkpoint subtree with N filtered-out blobs cost N `git cat-file -e`
subprocesses before any fetch happened — explain.go's own spinner comment
admitted this "can take seconds on a deep checkpoint subtree".

Split the walk from the verdict: gather the storer misses, then settle the
whole set with a single `git cat-file --batch-check`, which prints
"<oid> missing" for what it cannot find. Order and duplicates are preserved,
and a probe that cannot run still reports every candidate as missing — the
direction the per-hash check already failed in, and the safe one (a candidate
wrongly called missing costs one batched fetch; one wrongly called present
sends File() back to a per-blob fetch).

GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH stays load-bearing and moves to the batched command:
--batch-check batches the lookups, not the promisor fetches. Measured on a
promisor clone with 5 missing blobs, `cat-file --batch-check` without the
variable spawns 5 `git fetch --stdin` children and then reports every blob
present; with it, zero.

Tests: one subprocess for a 3-candidate tree, carrying GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1,
returning exactly the blob whose loose object was deleted; every candidate kept
when the probe cannot run. The treeless-explain integration test now pins
--batch-check and asserts no per-blob `-e` probe reappears.

cd2619d3129ae4ea95e11af83ab4b609e63d0761
fix(checkpoint): pass --no-optional-locks to every git status

`git status` is a write, not a read. It refreshes the index's stat cache
and, when any entry is stale, takes .git/index.lock for the whole
worktree walk and renames a fresh index over .git/index. That is git
working as designed, and running `git status` from the checkpoint path
was not wrong. What makes the write not worth its cost is that Entire
gets nothing from it: every call site reads the porcelain output once and
discards it, so the stat-cache update is pure overhead. Output is
byte-identical with the flag.

The overhead only becomes visible on a filesystem where
rename-over-existing is not atomic against a concurrent lookup — virtiofs
/ gRPC-FUSE bind mounts, i.e. Docker Desktop devcontainers. There a
concurrent reader can observe ENOENT on .git/index; git silently treats
ENOENT, and only ENOENT, as an *empty* index; and a `git commit` landing
in that window records the empty tree with exit code 0 and no warning —
a commit that deletes every tracked file (#2111).

Measured on a virtiofs bind mount vs ext4, same writer and reader:

  virtiofs   29,596 opens   2,939 ENOENT (9.9%)   12,545 renames
  ext4    1,930,880 opens       0 ENOENT         199,846 renames

and end to end, with the reporter's add/commit workflow racing the
writer:

  virtiofs, plain git status        11 empty-tree commits / 615 attempts
  ext4, plain git status             0 / 2630
  virtiofs, --no-optional-locks      0 / 394

This does not eliminate the hazard and should not be described as if it
did. On an affected mount any concurrent `git status` opens the same
window — the user's own, another tool's, a file watcher's, and in
particular several agents working the same repo, each running its own
hooks. Our share is the one write that is both unnecessary and
asynchronous to the human's terminal, so it is the one that can land
between someone's `git add` and their `git commit`. For the writers we do
not control the mitigation is GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 in the environment,
which covers every git process in the session.

Also fixed at the same call site: the subprocess inherited GIT_DIR /
GIT_WORK_TREE / GIT_INDEX_FILE from the enclosing git hook, and those
take precedence over cmd.Dir — so it could resolve a different repo
entirely. strategy's private env scrubber moves to
gitrepo.EnvWithoutRepoOverrides so checkpoint can share it without an
import cycle. Not applied to user-invoked commands that act on the
current directory, where a GIT_DIR the user exported is an instruction
rather than contamination.

Verified against the reproducing environment with the real binary: the
shipped build replaces .git/index on a single stop hook, the patched
build leaves it untouched, and the resulting checkpoint trees are
identical across modified / new / deleted / renamed / spaces / nested /
mtime-only changes.

The guard test exists instead of a comment because this exact producer
was diagnosed once before (ENT-242, Feb 2026) and the knowledge left the
codebase: the fix was closed unmerged on the false premise that
`git status --porcelain -z` "reads without rewriting", and would have
grown the number of index-rewriting call sites from one to eleven.

fix(review): bound judge CLI call so a pipe-holding grandchild can't hang it

`entire review` could hang indefinitely at "Final judge is consolidating"
past its 20-minute deadline. The judge runs through
RunIsolatedTextGeneratorCLI, which spawned the provider CLI with
exec.CommandContext and captured output into buffers. When the deadline
fired it killed only the direct child; the child's grandchildren (a
sandbox/MCP helper) kept the output pipe open, so the stdout/stderr copy
goroutines never saw EOF and cmd.Run blocked forever — the deadline was
silently defeated.
