fix(strategy): stop a dead capture locking out re-capture

Two rules read the same state and disagreed about what it means. The resolver asks
whether a captured remote is actually configured and skips it if not, falling
through to origin. maybeCapture only asked whether the file was non-empty.

So `git remote rename fork myfork` stranded it: the resolver skipped the dead
`fork` entry and elected origin, while the sticky check still saw a non-empty file
and refused to ever capture `myfork`. Reproduced end to end — after the rename,
a push to the now-declared `myfork` captured nothing and the state file stayed
{"remotes":["fork"]} indefinitely.

Worse than "routes to origin": for a user who only pushes to `myfork`, every push
is gated (myfork != origin), so checkpoints reach nowhere and accumulate locally.
Nothing surfaces why. saveCapturedSyncRemotes has one production caller and
nothing else touches the file — `entire clean` deliberately leaves it — so the only
recovery was deleting a file we never mention.

The sticky check now asks the resolver's question. A live capture still blocks
(verified: with myfork captured, a push to a third remote does not move the
election, so first-capture-sticks holds); only a dead one unblocks. The state file
prunes itself because save overwrites, so no separate cleanup is needed. All 13
existing capture subtests pass unchanged, including "existing capture sticks" and
"corrupt capture state falls through" — nothing depended on presence semantics.

Reported by Peyton Montei.

mechanism in the direction that matters: it credits the push and omits the

looser, unsafe mechanism. It was also plural about a single event: first capture
sticks.

than the bookkeeping — "follows your branch's push destination". Renaming the enum
is free because it is introduced by this PR and has never shipped; nothing
external can be keyed on it yet.

maybeCaptureCheckpointSyncRemote, loadCapturedSyncRemotes) — "capture" is a fair
name for the latch as an implementation concept, and the constant's doc now
records why the user-facing label differs so the mismatch does not read as an
oversight.

fix(strategy): give the capture state file a unique temp path

saveCapturedSyncRemotes staged through a fixed `<path>.tmp`. That file lives in
the git common dir, which is shared by every worktree of the repo, so two
concurrent pre-push hooks write the same scratch path — and one can rename the
other's half-written content into place, or rename a file the other has since
truncated.

os.CreateTemp in the same directory gives each writer its own scratch name. The
0600 mode is preserved explicitly (CreateTemp opens 0600 already, but the chmod
keeps the intent local to the code rather than resting on that), and cleanup is
deferred so every failure path removes its temp instead of leaving debris beside
the real file.

The check-then-write sequence in maybeCaptureCheckpointSyncRemote is still not
atomic — two concurrent first captures can both observe "nothing captured" and
both write. With first-capture-sticks that makes the winner nondeterministic
rather than corrupt, so it is left alone here; the push queue in the same
directory takes an flock for its equivalent, which is the shape to follow if this
needs to become exclusive.

fix(logging): set the cobra traverse flag at init, not per root command

EnableTraverseRunHooks is a global in the cobra package, and NewRootCmd wrote it
on every construction. Parallel tests build and execute root commands
concurrently, so that write raced both other writes and cobra reading the flag
during Execute — 12 race reports in CI, which then failed ~40 unrelated tests in
the same binary because the detector aborts the whole run.

and nothing for a future caller to get wrong. sync.Once would not have been
enough — it orders the writes against each other but not against a reader in
another goroutine that never calls it.

refactor(strategy): converge identity linking on proclive, delete proctree

Trail review (1061) found internal/proctree duplicating the existing
proclive package: same ancestry walk, same per-platform introspection
(one sysctl/stat parse apart), and — decisively — proclive's Identity is
already persisted on EVERY turn start as SessionState.Owner by
captureSessionOwner, seven lines from where this branch re-walked the
same process tree into a second field. The review also showed the
duplicate's Windows walker ran in no CI job (the Windows job filters on
test names carrying Windows/MSYS; none did), had an orphan-reparenting
hazard PID recycling makes real, cost one process-table snapshot per
ancestry level, and that the shell filter was missing "entire" and "go"
— both already on proclive's transient list.

Converge instead of duplicating:

- proclive gains HasAncestor(Identity) — the commit-attribution
  question ("was this process spawned, however indirectly, by the
  recorded owner?") with proclive's host, boot, and start-fingerprint
  guards, so a recycled PID or an identity recorded on another machine
  can never match — two guards the deleted package lacked (its own doc
  conceded the Linux cross-reboot collision that proclive's bootID
  closes). Plus IdentityOf(pid) for callers and tests.

  HasAncestor. No new recording, no AgentAncestry field, no
  refreshAgentAncestry (Owner is re-captured every turn start, which
  already covers resume under a new agent process). Ties — one agent
  process hosting several sessions, or a nested agent whose outer agent
  is also an ancestor — go to the most recently interacting session.
- internal/proctree is deleted. On platforms proclive cannot introspect
  (Windows), identity matching reports nothing and linking falls back
  to worktree matching — honestly, rather than via platform code no CI
  job executed.

owner-matching compares first-non-transient identities and breaks when
a non-transient wrapper interposes at commit time; HasAncestor's

11773e1e37f2411ee096f4e72cda55d3c12b6e4c
fix(checkpoint): address review findings on the read-remotes chain

High severity:

- Attach's local-presence gates are local-only again. The read chain
  selects per checkpoint across local and remote-tracking trees, so a
  stale-but-existing local v1 branch fell through to origin's tracking
  tree and reported a checkpoint "present" that the next local write
  would not build on — the exact clobber the gate exists to prevent
  ("Only local presence counts"). New PersistentRefs.PrimaryAsLocalRead
  pins reads to the local ref with no remote tiers; both attach guards
  use it. The main attach store meanwhile gains the read chain it was
  missing, so informational reads reach the elected remote.

- Checkpoint-ref hydration no longer installs a legacy tip under
  elected-remote uncertainty. FetchCheckpointRefFrom installs the
  canonical LOCAL ref (+ref:ref); checkpoint refs advance (backfills
  parent onto the tip); and hydration only runs when the ref is absent
  locally — so falling through to origin while the elected remote (the
  only remote writes confine to) was merely unreachable permanently
  installed a possibly-stale tip. The chain now advances only on
  authoritative absence; transport failure aborts. The git-branch
  read path is unchanged (pure tree reads install nothing), and the
  integration matrix now pins the split per backend.

- A FAILED election with a missing local primary seeds from origin's
  real history instead of a fresh orphan. Checkpoint pushes are already
  fail-closed while the election is broken, so the orphan bought no
  safety — but it guaranteed a disjoint history (non-fast-forward on
  every sync) the moment the user fixed checkpoint_push_remote. Seeding
  a MISSING ref is not the #1374 replay-on-divergence hazard; the
  elected-exists confinement pin is unchanged.

Medium severity:

- agentimport's idempotency listing consults the read chain
  (Options.ReadRemotes, wired by both callers): turns already on the
  elected remote were re-imported, turns only in origin's stale
  tracking ref were wrongly skipped.
- GetCheckpointAuthor iterates the same chain as content reads, so
  explain no longer shows an empty author for checkpoints whose commit
  lives only on a remote tier.
- checkpointpolicy.SyncFrom reports the ENFORCED (local) policy when a
  read-only legacy baseline could not advance the local ref, instead of
  printing a policy the hooks never enforce; the unadopted baseline
  stays visible via RemoteHash.
- The resume metadata fetch skips already-present legacy tracking refs
  after a successful elected fetch (bootstrap-only), halving steady-
  state deep fetches; a fresh clone still bootstraps origin's legacy
  tier once.
- resolveSessionsBranchTrees skips candidates whose commit is an
  ancestor of an already-kept tree, eliminating the duplicate shard
  walk when the local branch is ahead of a tracking ref.

Deferred with rationale: making OpenOptions.ReadRemotes self-derivable
inside checkpoint.Open (finding: hand-threading at ~15 sites) requires
checkpoint to import strategy — an import cycle. The explicit wiring
plus the attach fix above is the practical mitigation; revisit if the
chain resolver ever moves below the checkpoint package.

The initial fix skipped two injected prefixes when picking a session title,

always injected, in five shapes: an AGENTS.md dump (107), <environment_context>
(46), <recommended_plugins> (8), <user_action> (2), and <turn_aborted> (1).

agent boilerplate — <user_action> among them, whose content begins "User
initiated a review task", i.e. exactly the agent_review flow ENT-1653 reports.

The prefix list also existed twice: compact.isCodexSystemContent carried six
prefixes, strategy's predicate three. That drift was the bug. Collapse both
onto one classifier, textutil.IsInjectedPrompt, covering the union plus the
three newly observed shapes. Measured over the same 164 rollouts, sessions
titled with injected content go 164 (before any filter) -> 12 -> 4, and those
4 contain no genuine prompt at all, so the raw-preamble fallback is correct.

f86f8a42c541d9ee760bc3e27105168dafe534e1
feat(strategy): link commits to sessions by process identity

Commit-to-session linking guessed by worktree path: the commit hooks
matched SessionState.WorktreePath against the commit's worktree. Any
drift between that bookkeeping and reality lost the linkage — an agent
committing in a sibling worktree produced an unlinked commit, or worse:
with a poisoned state dir, a wrong link. Both happened for real (three
retro-attach incidents; most recently a leaked test fixture session,
sessC, was linked to a commit and stamped a dangling trailer whose
checkpoint was never written).

Identity-first linking removes the guessing for agent commits. At
session start the hook records its nearest process ancestors
(pid + start time; the agent process is among them, since agents run
hooks as children) in SessionState.AgentAncestry. At commit time the
hook walks its own ancestry (git <- tool shell <- agent) and matches
those refs: nearest ancestor wins, ties go to the most recently
interacting session, start times guard against PID reuse. The identity
match is UNIONED with the worktree-matched set, never a replacement —
a commit condenses every session with pending content in its worktree,
and identity adds the one that path matching missed.

A commit identity-matched outside the session's home worktree is
guest-linked: condensed and linked, but worktree-coupled state
(BaseCommit, shadow-branch realignment) is never mutated from a foreign
worktree — shadow branches are keyed by BaseCommit + WorktreeID, and
the session's next home commit must still match.

The worktree fallback (human commits, severed process trees) is
hardened in the same pass:

- Imported sessions never link: they are historical records, and a
  leaked imported fixture is exactly what hijacked the sessC commit.
- Multi-worktree ambiguity is filtered to sessions that interacted
  within the last 15 minutes; a single live worktree links, two live
  worktrees still decline — now with a stderr hint naming
  'entire session adopt' instead of only a log-level warning.

And the leak that poisoned the state dir is closed at both ends:
agent import scopes its session-state store to the repo being imported
into (new session.NewStateStoreForWorktree) instead of the process CWD,
and under 'go test' the CWD-resolved store refuses to open outside the
temp root, so any future non-isolated test fails loudly instead of
writing fixtures into a developer's real .git/entire-sessions. The full
unit suite passes with the guard on — the agentimport tests were the
only leakers.

New internal/proctree package: cross-platform process ancestry
(darwin sysctl, linux /proc, windows toolhelp) with pid+starttime
identity.

re-redacted it from byte zero. On a 70MB Codex rollout that was ~67s per Stop

appended. Two properties make the splice sound:

  - Redaction is per-line and stateless, so redact(A+B) == redact(A)+redact(B).

  - A stored prefix always ends immediately after a newline, so the redacted
    prefix does too and plain byte concatenation reproduces the full result with
    no boundary fixups. Content with a partial trailing line is never stored.

matches, so a rewritten or compacted transcript, changed custom rules, or a CLI
upgrade all fall back to redacting everything. The fingerprint mixes the CLI
version and commit into redact.ConfigFingerprint as a conservative proxy for the
vendored ruleset, which is not introspectable: an upgrade costs one full redaction.

A caller that caches redacted bytes needs to know when the bytes were produced

the custom-rule set (inline plus rule packs, sorted so map order cannot leak into
the hash) and the PII layer's enablement, per-category toggles, and user patterns.

pattern, a different placeholder token, or a change to how regions are merged.

bytes must never be shared between OPF and non-OPF paths; and the betterleaks
ruleset version, which the library does not expose, so a caller that caches across

1ac6a1e37e1fc8ed67cb05320260f6bf8006a3f8
perf(redact): shard JSONL line redaction across goroutines

Redaction is the dominant cost of storing a large transcript: profiling the
checkpoint blob write put it at ~99.7% of the total (git object writing was
174ms of a 66.7s pass on 70MB), and 82% of that is betterleaks' regex ruleset
under Go's NFA engine.

Every line is redacted in isolation by a stateless redactor, so the line pass can
be split. Shard it and rejoin in order; output is byte-identical.

Shards are sized by bytes rather than one-per-core, for two reasons. Per-byte cost
climbs with input size (allocation and GC pressure over one large buffer), so
small pieces are cheaper per byte *and* run concurrently -- measured on a 20MB
Codex transcript, 43s sequential vs 2.1s across 12 shards, which is superlinear in
shard count and not explainable by parallelism alone. And balancing by bytes
rather than line count matters because agent transcripts mix thousands of short
lines with occasional multi-MB tool results, where equal line counts would leave
one oversized shard as the tail.

Sharding is gated on an explicit argument describing the redactor, not on which
entry point the caller reached. String is pure and opts in; the OPF flow's
collector closures accumulate into a shared map and slice and opt out. Stating it
per call site is what lets batch.go's OPF-disabled fast path -- the same pure
String redactor over whole transcript blobs -- take the win too.

Also preallocates the line builder from the input size (4.5x on a 1MiB shard,
which helps the sequential path as well).

Verified safe to share the layer config across goroutines: the betterleaks
Detect path does not mutate the shared detector (all mutation is confined to
Run), and the custom-rule, PII, and detector globals are sync.Once/RWMutex
guarded. Tests assert sharded output equals sequential across a fixture that
exercises every layer, plus shard boundaries, edge shapes, and the
redact(A+B) == redact(A)+redact(B) property that callers splitting a transcript
depend on. Passes -race.

0a833207fa94de3d912f6589785913e51647f314
perf(checkpoint): stop the remote cache serializing cross-repository git reads

The cache held its single mutex across the git subprocess, not just the map
access. `entire dispatch --repos a,b` fans out over repositories with an errgroup
(dispatch/mode_local.go:109), so every repository's git read queued behind every
other's — serializing work that ran concurrently before this cache existed. The
per-repository partitioning added in f6770e793 gave each repo its own entry but
they all still contended on one lock.

Locking is now two-level: gitRemoteCache.mu guards only the byDir map and is
never held across an exec, and each repository's answers sit behind their own
mutex. Within one repository callers still serialize, which is the point for two
racing reads of the same key — the second waits and takes the memoized answer
instead of shelling out again. Two reads of different keys in one repository
serialize too; the key set is tiny (the remote list, plus membership for the
elected remote and origin), so that is a bounded cost for a much simpler
invariant than per-key locking.

Invalidation still just drops the map: a goroutine already holding a snapshot
finishes against it and its result is discarded with the old map rather than being
observed after the mutation.

TestGitRemoteCache_CrossRepoReadsDoNotSerialize pins it, ordered so the outcome
cannot depend on which goroutine starts first — A enters its read, and only then
is B allowed to call. Verified to fail (10s deadline) with the lock held across

fix(checkpoint): partition the remote cache per repository, and finish the chain

Addresses the three open findings on this trail.

and a single ordered slice, with no repository scoping, while `entire dispatch
--repos a,b` walks several repositories in ONE process — scoping each election
with settings.WithWorktreeRoot so the git calls run in that repo
(dispatch/mode_local.go, whose own comment says so). Repo B's election would have
answered from repo A's remote list, silently re-breaking c04a2e312 ("honor read
candidates per repository"). Answers are now partitioned by repository root:
the context's scoped worktree root when there is one, else the repo containing
the process working directory that git would inherit. The repo root rather than
the raw cwd because `git remote get-url` answers the same from any subdirectory,
so subdirectory calls should share one entry; paths.WorktreeRoot is memoized per
cwd, so the partition costs far less than the subprocess it protects. An
unidentifiable repository disables caching for that call rather than sharing
another's answers. Pinned by TestGitRemoteCache_PartitionsByRepository.

commands — naming `dispatch` and `runner --run` alongside `mcp` — "must scope
their own window", but only mcp does. With per-repository partitioning the
multi-repo correctness problem is structural rather than each caller's to
remember, so the comment now says what is actually true: partitioning handles
repository identity, per-request windows handle freshness over time, and mcp is
the one command that needs the latter today.

in this branch still opening without ReadRemotes, so `entire session resume`'s
logs-only path fell back to the legacy origin-only tier and could fail to find
metadata that resume/explain now read from a non-origin elected remote.

c32e8f23055d2864e540260bd76f1332cc252179
perf(checkpoint): bound the read chain and stop re-electing per call

Fixes two costs this PR's read-candidate chain introduced, both measured
against origin/main with a PATH-shimmed git counting subprocesses.

Unbounded worst case. Per-candidate budgets replaced single shared ones —
a real fix, since one shared budget let a hung leader starve the legacy
origin tier — but nothing bounded the total, and these read paths have no
outer deadline: `entire resume` sets none and main() uses
context.WithCancel, not WithTimeout. fetchBlobsByHash lost the most: it
used to run inside one 2-minute budget that also covered its fallback
fetches, and per-target budgets left those fallbacks on the caller's
uncapped context, so a stalled hydration could spend per-target budgets
and then a fresh per-candidate metadata chain on top.

ReadChainBudget now wraps all three chains — checkpoint ref hydration, the
metadata branch chain, and blob hydration including its fallbacks — with
per-candidate budgets nested inside, so every candidate keeps its own
window while the total stays bounded.

Sized as an absolute 3 minutes rather than "n tiers x one full window".
The multiple is the trap: at 2 x ReadFetchTimeout with today's two tiers
the ceiling equals the loop's own worst case, so it cannot bind and buys
nothing, and blob hydration's fallbacks inherit an already-expired
context. An absolute ceiling binds for every chain of two or more
candidates, leaves a single-candidate chain untouched, and does not go
quietly wrong when a third tier appears. ReadChainLoopBudget holds back a
sixth of it so the fallbacks are funded rather than merely inside it, and
ReadFetchTimeout is exported so the cli-side paths stop carrying their own
2-minute literals that had to stay silently equal to it.

Election cost per command. The election re-runs on every call by design,
and each run shells out to git twice over .git/config: which remotes
exist, and does remote X exist. One command elects several times —
`entire checkpoint list` resolves the chain four times (disconnection
warning, branch listing, the git-refs store's remote discovery, imported
rewind points), spending 15 git subprocesses where main spent 9.

WithGitRemoteCache memoizes only those two .git/config reads, installed on
the root context in main(). The election result, settings, and the
captured-election file stay uncached, so a write followed by a re-resolve
still sees the new value — #1991's capture keeps working, which caching the
election result would have silently broken. Context-scoped and opt-in, so
an uninstrumented context behaves exactly as before and tests cannot leak
one temp repo's remote list into another.

Process scope is not invocation scope for every command: `entire mcp`
serves an agent session from one context, so it installs a fresh cache per
request via WithFreshGitRemoteCache rather than pinning one snapshot of
"which remotes exist" for hours. `entire repo mirror use` is the only
git-remote mutation in the CLI and invalidates after its writes.

WarnIfMetadataDisconnected now takes the caller's context instead of
building context.Background(): the detached context ignored both interrupt
cancellation and the cache, re-shelling out for answers the caller already
had.

Measured, `entire checkpoint list`: main 9 subprocesses, this PR before
these changes 15, after 9 — the regression is fully recovered (1 config
--get-regexp and 2 remote get-url, same as main).

Tests: the ceiling test stalls every target under a production-shaped
ratio (ceiling below targets x per-target, which is what makes it bind)
and asserts the call returns in ~ceiling — 0.58s with the ceiling, 1.09s
and failing without. Cache tests cover opt-in behavior, empty lists as
real answers, negative caching, invalidation, and an end-to-end guard that
a remote added mid-invocation is visible to a later election after
invalidation.

2661867ad980f4f63d44ab9cefe98bef57688ec4
feat(strategy): capture the checkpoint sync remote from tracked pushes

The single-remote election (ENT-1451) guesses the sync destination from
config at rest — origin, else sole, else first in .git/config — so a user
whose branches push a non-origin remote had checkpoints strand locally
until they hand-configured checkpoint_push_remote. First user report
landed the day after v0.10.0 shipped.

Capture makes the election follow demonstrated push behavior with zero
configuration: during pre-push, a push whose target agrees with the
branch's declared push destination (branch.<name>.pushRemote ->
remote.pushDefault -> branch.<name>.remote — the config a bare
'git push' resolves through) and differs from the current election
persists that remote as the captured election, announces it on stderr,
and the same push carries the checkpoints. The captured tier sits
between the explicit setting and origin, and is fail-soft: a captured
remote that was renamed or removed falls through to the default tiers
instead of disabling sync.

Neither signal elects alone. Declaration without a push is the
config-at-rest bug that got the static tracking tier dropped (74e239a9:
a 'clone -o base' stranded every origin push); a push without
declaration is the pre-single-remote transcript leak (a one-off
'git push upstream' must never publish transcripts). Capture acts only
on their intersection.

Phase-1 rules: at most one captured remote and the first capture sticks,
so a mixed-habit repo whose branches push two remotes cannot flip the
election on every push. The state file is list-shaped from day one so
the multi-remote set (per-remote push-queue tracking) needs no
migration. An explicit checkpoint_push_remote outranks and disables
capture.

The existing single-remote integration tests set up their gated remote
with 'push -u', which under capture is a declared destination — their
setups now reset tracking so they keep pinning the undeclared-one-off
shape, and TestCheckpointSyncRemote_BranchTrackingDoesNotReroute is
split into its two surviving truths: tracking alone still never reroutes
(the 74e239a9 regression pin), and a tracked push now legitimately
captures.

Merge note: reads still resolve through origin until the read-side stack
(#1956/#1951) lands; this PR must merge after it so captured non-origin
elections are readable end to end.

fix(hooks): bound the agent-hook status walk so pathological repos degrade instead of hanging

go-git's Worktree.Status walks the whole worktree and is not
context-cancellable. On a pathological repo (live incident: a stray
`git init` in $HOME with no .gitignore) the walk ground for hours in
hook processes that outlived the agent's ~60s hook timeout — two
zombies at ~1.8GB RSS, one with 25 CPU-minutes — while the failure
stayed completely silent: no session state, no checkpoint, no log line.

Add gitrepo.StatusWithBudget: a 20s wall-clock budget (headroom under
the agent timeout for the rest of the capture path) enforced by a
goroutine+select wrapper that abandons the walk on breach — the
orphaned goroutine dies with the one-shot hook process, which is the
point. On breach it returns an error wrapping
gitrepo.ErrStatusBudgetExceeded, emits an actionable Warn naming the
repo root, elapsed, budget, and consequence, and latches a
process-local flag so no later walk in the same hook process re-enters
the worktree (the turn-start hook walks twice: pre-prompt capture and
prompt attribution).

Route the agent-hook call sites through it — DetectFileChanges
(turn-end, subagent-end, PostTodo), the pre-prompt/pre-task untracked
scans, and the prompt-attribution walk — and make the pre-prompt/
pre-task captures fail open on status errors instead of failing the
hook: capture proceeds with transcript-derived data, and a new
UntrackedScanSkipped marker tells the paired end-hook to skip new-file
detection so pre-existing untracked files are not misattributed to the
agent. Git-hook paths (post-commit condensation) never call Status;
review/rewind keep the unbounded Status since a user is actively
waiting there.

feat(codex): finalize sessions via Codex's SessionEnd hook

Codex gained a SessionEnd hook in 0.146 (openai/codex#33895, "Add SessionEnd
hooks for thread teardown"). Until now Entire only registered SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, Stop and PostToolUse, so quitting Codex left the session
un-finalized and it showed up in `entire status` indefinitely.

Register it, parse it into the normalized SessionEnd event, and include it in
install/uninstall/detection. The payload is thinner than Codex's other hooks —
no model, permission_mode or turn_id — and its `reason` is a constant, so only
session_id, cwd and transcript_path are consumed.

The hook is subject to a ceiling the others are not: Codex defaults SessionEnd
handlers to 1s and clamps them to 3s (SESSION_END_MAX_TIMEOUT_SEC), warning at
every startup when a config asks for more, then terminates the hook's process
tree on expiry. So hook timeouts become per-event — SessionEnd at exactly the
ceiling, everything else unchanged at 30s — and the command match now includes
the timeout so a hook installed by an older Entire is rewritten rather than
left to nag.

Agents in that position declare a budget through the new optional
SessionEndBudgeter interface, which bounds only the eager condense.
Mark-ended stays unbounded: it is one atomic state-file rename and must always
complete. The bound is best-effort — condensation does not poll ctx between
stages — and exists to stop short of the process-tree kill, not to make
condensation interruptible. Either way of being cut off is safe, since
MutateSessionState persists at the end and PostCommit retries.

6cacb0ce53acde22292ca4d79ff0b2fd5efa5444
fix(session): reclaim IDLE sessions whose agent process exited

State.OwnerExited gated on Phase.IsActive(), which is only PhaseActive. An
agent that finishes its last turn transitions ACTIVE -> IDLE, so a session
whose agent then quit without firing a session-end hook was invisible to the
dead-owner sweep in `entire status` and `entire doctor`.

That is exactly the shape Codex leaves behind — it had no SessionEnd hook
before 0.146 — and it can happen to any agent that is killed before its hook
runs. Those sessions lingered as "active" for 7 days until StaleSessionThreshold
made StateStore.Load delete the state file outright, discarding pending
checkpoint work rather than condensing it.

Process death is unambiguous and phase-independent, so OwnerExited now excludes
only already-finalized sessions (PhaseEnded or EndedAt set). doctor's
classifySession checks it ahead of the phase switch for the same reason; the
repeated stuckSession literals collapse into a local constructor.

The previous commit removed GetLastUserPrompt, GetLastAssistantResponse,
TruncateAtUUID and FindToolResultUUID from AgentSession. Those four were
the only readers of the normalized-entry model, so what it left behind
was a data shape with no writer and no reader: the Entries field,

cursor, external, factoryaidroid, geminicli, opencode, pi, vogon) plus
resume.go and strategy/manual_commit_pending.go - and none sets Entries.

assert its fields read back, which the compiler already guarantees.

The field's comment offered it as an extension point ("agents may
populate this if needed"), but it was never wired up to be one: the
external plugin wire format, AgentSessionJSON in agent/external/types.go,
carries no entries field, so an out-of-tree agent cannot populate it
either. Removing the model breaks no in-tree caller and no protocol
surface.

Kept, and still worth a human's call: GetSessionID and ReadSession are
implemented ten times and invoked through the agent.Agent interface zero
times, but they back the get-session-id and read-session verbs of the
external plugin protocol, so shrinking the interface is a contract change

Define the pending dataset as both halves it actually contains

Answers five Copilot review comments on #2187. Four are one theme and
Copilot is right about it: my definition said a pending checkpoint "has
not yet been condensed onto entire/checkpoints/v1", which is true of only
half the dataset. The strategy.go type doc contradicted itself inside a
single sentence -- "not yet condensed... : either live shadow-branch state
or a logs-only point" -- because a logs-only point is precisely one that
HAS been condensed.

What ListLogsOnlyPendingCheckpoints actually builds: it scans the current
branch's history for commits carrying an Entire-Checkpoint trailer, and
keeps the ones whose trailer resolves against *committed* checkpoint
storage. The row's ID is that branch commit, CheckpointID is the condensed
checkpoint on v1, IsLogsOnly is true. It is listed so the session
transcript can be restored from v1 via RestoreLogsOnly -- file state would
need a git checkout. So it is derived from condensed history, not from
un-condensed work, and ListPendingCheckpoints merges it with the live
shadow-branch rows and sorts the two together by date.

One definition, adapted per context: `checkpoint list --pending` is the
resume view of the current branch, and a row is either a live checkpoint
on the session's shadow branch (not yet condensed) or a logs-only resume
point recovered from a commit whose logs already are. "Pending" names the
listing, not a property every row has.

hooks and no session. Holding review's argv fixed and varying one flag:
--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust yields 5 hooks and a tagged session,

Bound the sweep's condensing. Widening OwnerExited to IDLE multiplied the
candidate set — IDLE is the resting state, so the sweep now catches every agent
quit at its prompt, not just ones killed mid-turn — and each candidate triggered
a deadline-free condense inside `entire status`. Measured, one condense is
~120ms floor and seconds for a real transcript, against a 40ms command, serially
and uncapped; with a 7-day StaleSessionThreshold the first sweep after upgrade
drains a week's backlog in one stall, and `--json` (the MCP entire_status tool)
prints nothing until it finishes. sweepCondenseBudget now caps condensing across
the whole sweep while every candidate is still marked ENDED, which is what
actually un-sticks it from `entire status`. A new test pins that split.

Reuse and simplification, no behaviour change:
- Hoist the "already finalized" rule to State.IsEnded(); it was spelled out at
  three sites whose comments claimed they were kept in sync by hand.
- Collapse codex's parseSessionStart/parseSessionEnd into parseSessionInfoEvent
  over one sessionInfoRaw, matching geminicli and factoryaidroid, which solved
  the same "these differ only in event type" problem.
- Drive codex's hooks.json handling from a managedHooks table. Install,
  uninstall and detection each repeated the same five-event block, so adding
  SessionEnd was a 12-line edit across three functions with three chances to
  miss one; the per-event timeout now lives with the event.

  lazy-init dance, pair SetLogLevelGetter with EnsureInitialized (without it
  the sweep ignored log_level in settings), drop an unreachable error branch,

- Fold duplicated tests into tables; derive expected hook counts from the table.

  could not enforce a budget itself — the work runs in the entire process.

433103a7c492758678b370740a064e516d131746
feat(codex): finalize sessions via Codex's SessionEnd hook

Codex gained a SessionEnd hook in 0.146 (openai/codex#33895, "Add SessionEnd
hooks for thread teardown"). Until now Entire only registered SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, Stop and PostToolUse, so quitting Codex left the session
un-finalized and it showed up in `entire status` indefinitely.

Register it, parse it into the normalized SessionEnd event, and include it in
install/uninstall/detection. The payload is thinner than Codex's other hooks —
no model, permission_mode or turn_id — and its `reason` is a constant, so only
session_id, cwd and transcript_path are consumed.

The hook is subject to a ceiling the others are not: Codex defaults SessionEnd
handlers to 1s and clamps them to 3s (SESSION_END_MAX_TIMEOUT_SEC), warning at
every startup when a config asks for more, then terminates the hook's process
tree on expiry. So hook timeouts become per-event — SessionEnd at exactly the
ceiling, everything else unchanged at 30s — and the command match now includes
the timeout so a hook installed by an older Entire is rewritten rather than
left to nag.

Agents in that position declare a budget through the new optional
SessionEndBudgeter interface, which bounds only the eager condense.
Mark-ended stays unbounded: it is one atomic state-file rename and must always
complete. The bound is best-effort — condensation does not poll ctx between
stages — and exists to stop short of the process-tree kill, not to make
condensation interruptible. Either way of being cut off is safe, since
MutateSessionState persists at the end and PostCommit retries.

6cacb0ce53acde22292ca4d79ff0b2fd5efa5444
fix(session): reclaim IDLE sessions whose agent process exited

State.OwnerExited gated on Phase.IsActive(), which is only PhaseActive. An
agent that finishes its last turn transitions ACTIVE -> IDLE, so a session
whose agent then quit without firing a session-end hook was invisible to the
dead-owner sweep in `entire status` and `entire doctor`.

That is exactly the shape Codex leaves behind — it had no SessionEnd hook
before 0.146 — and it can happen to any agent that is killed before its hook
runs. Those sessions lingered as "active" for 7 days until StaleSessionThreshold
made StateStore.Load delete the state file outright, discarding pending
checkpoint work rather than condensing it.

Process death is unambiguous and phase-independent, so OwnerExited now excludes
only already-finalized sessions (PhaseEnded or EndedAt set). doctor's
classifySession checks it ahead of the phase switch for the same reason; the
repeated stuckSession literals collapse into a local constructor.

docs(security): qualify phone PII redaction as NANP-only

phone PII redaction is on by default whenever PII redaction is enabled, but
only matches North American (NANP) formats. The docs gave it no locale
qualifier, so a non-US user reading `phone: true` / `[REDACTED_PHONE]`
reasonably concludes phone numbers are stripped when for their own country's
numbers nothing happens. The table already qualifies `address` the same way.

Also notes that `[REDACTED_ADDRESS]` replaces the street line only, so city,
state, and ZIP/postcode survive, and points users needing other locales at
`custom_patterns`.

Docs only; no change to the matchers.

433103a7c492758678b370740a064e516d131746
feat(codex): finalize sessions via Codex's SessionEnd hook

Codex gained a SessionEnd hook in 0.146 (openai/codex#33895, "Add SessionEnd
hooks for thread teardown"). Until now Entire only registered SessionStart,
UserPromptSubmit, Stop and PostToolUse, so quitting Codex left the session
un-finalized and it showed up in `entire status` indefinitely.

Register it, parse it into the normalized SessionEnd event, and include it in
install/uninstall/detection. The payload is thinner than Codex's other hooks —
no model, permission_mode or turn_id — and its `reason` is a constant, so only
session_id, cwd and transcript_path are consumed.

The hook is subject to a ceiling the others are not: Codex defaults SessionEnd
handlers to 1s and clamps them to 3s (SESSION_END_MAX_TIMEOUT_SEC), warning at
every startup when a config asks for more, then terminates the hook's process
tree on expiry. So hook timeouts become per-event — SessionEnd at exactly the
ceiling, everything else unchanged at 30s — and the command match now includes
the timeout so a hook installed by an older Entire is rewritten rather than
left to nag.

Agents in that position declare a budget through the new optional

{"base":{"ref":"main","sha":"c7a96436dc255d55b885dd80bed2f6809d90a748"},"body":"## Problem

`process_sessions` still persists each session separately. For every session, it reloads the checkpoint, rebuilds the session index and summary, creates a commit, and advances the checkpoint ref.

Issue #2091 measures that work at roughly 73–103 ms per session. The repeated checkpoint load and rebuild make condensation slower as more sessions share a checkpoint.

Checkpoint-level batching needs two things first:

- Ref updates must detect concurrent writes from hooks, worktrees, CLI processes, and other Git clients.
- Both persistent Git layouts must use the same batch algorithm.

## Solution

This PR adds native compare-and-swap publication and a shared `BatchSessions` write request.

It lays the storage and concurrency groundwork for #2091 item 2. It does not yet change PostCommit to group and submit sessions in batches. That work is listed below.

## Native compare-and-swap publication

`CompareAndSwapRef` publishes refs through native Git:

```text
git update-ref <ref> <new> <expected-old>
```

Missing-ref creation passes the correct all-zero object ID in both SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories.

`RunRefTransaction` retries a logical mutation when another writer wins the race. Each attempt reads the current tip, rebuilds from that tip, and publishes with CAS. Conflicts use bounded, cancellation-aware jitter. The transaction stops after 16 attempts.

A mutation that reports `changed=false` is an idempotent no-op and does not call `git update-ref`.

The CAS conversion covers persistent v1 metadata refs and per-checkpoint refs, including:

- initial ref creation;
- v1 migration;
- attribution, summary, and transcript backfills;
- reconciliation and safe local ref advancement;
- orphan cleanup and expected-old deletion;
- shadow-branch migration;
- rewind publication;
- OPF publication.

OPF uses one CAS attempt by design. If its expected ref has moved, it fails closed and withholds the push. It does not rebuild sanitized output from newly appeared content.

Go-git object construction now takes a process-local lock keyed by `*git.Repository`. This protects go-git state shared by concurrent writers in one process. Native Git CAS handles publication conflicts between processes.

## Checkpoint-level batch writes

`BatchSessions` is now part of the sealed `WriteRequest` union. One request contains a checkpoint ID and one or more reserved session writes.

Validation happens before object construction:

- The checkpoint ID must be present and valid.
- Every session must reference that checkpoint.
- Session IDs must be valid and unique.
- Sessions are sorted by `SessionID`.
- Task tool-use IDs and agent IDs must be valid.
- Duplicate task IDs within or across incoming sessions are rejected.
- Sessions without timestamps share one UTC timestamp, truncated to seconds.
- Author fallback, commit-message inputs, and prepared tree hashes are fixed before CAS retries.

`GitStore` and `gitRefsStore` share the same preparation and checkpoint-tree builder. Their wrappers only locate or splice the checkpoint subtree and choose the ref to publish.

For each CAS attempt, the builder:

- loads the existing checkpoint once;
- reads each existing session’s metadata once;
- reuses the numeric index when updating a session;
- preserves untouched session subtree hashes;
- appends new sessions in canonical order;
- merges the task subtree once and preserves untouched tasks;
- reduces the complete final session set into the root summary;
- preserves combined attribution and sticky review, investigation, and import flags;
- aggregates counts, tokens, files, strategy, branch, and commit SHA deterministically;
- creates one checkpoint commit for that backend attempt.

Existing `Session` and `ReservedSession` requests pass through the same builder with one session. Their caller contract does not change.

Combined attribution stays in its existing backfill transaction. The batch write does not fold it into the checkpoint commit.

## Storage and compatibility

The durable checkpoint format does not change:

```text
metadata.json
0/metadata.json
0/full.jsonl
0/transcript.jsonl
1/...
tasks/<tool-use-id>/...
```

Older clients already understand checkpoints with multiple numbered session directories. A batch produces the same tree, task subtree, summary, and metadata types that repeated single-session writes produce.

Compatibility was checked in separate dimensions:

- New clients continue to read existing checkpoint data.
- Old clients can read checkpoints written by `BatchSessions`.
- Existing callers still use `Writer.Write(context.Context, WriteRequest)`.
- Single-session requests keep their existing behavior.
- Malformed or ambiguous requests now fail before publication.
- Concurrent upgraded writers protect each other with native CAS.
- If an old blind writer publishes first, the CAS writer detects the change and rebuilds.
- If an old blind writer publishes second, it can still overwrite the newer write. One upgraded participant cannot make a pre-CAS writer safe.

Rejecting invalid input and replacing last-writer-wins behavior with conflict detection are intentional safety changes, not storage incompatibilities.

## Routing and partial success

Persistent dispatch, kind routing, fanout, and the filesystem test store support `BatchSessions`.

One Git backend makes every session in the batch visible through one ref update. Fanout writes the primary first. Mirror failures remain logged and best-effort, so they do not turn a successful primary write into an error.

Routing follows the backend encoded by the checkpoint ID if configuration changes after reservation. If a readable migrated copy exists, routing updates that copy too. The read-preferred backend is probed before the first physical write.

There is no transaction across physical backends. If the second backend fails, the first may already contain the batch. The writer returns the error. Retrying the same canonical upsert repairs the lagging copy.

A future lifecycle caller must therefore treat an error as “some backend may already contain this batch,” not as proof that nothing was written.

The filesystem store replaces one JSON document atomically under a process-local mutex. It is a test backend and does not provide cross-process serialization.

## Complexity

The deterministic visitation test uses existing checkpoints with 100, 200, and 500 sessions. With no tasks, it records:

```text
root entries visited          N + 1
session entries visited       N
existing metadata reads       N
task entries visited          0
final-session contributions   N
total                         4N + 1
```

These counters measure visits to checkpoint content, not every CPU operation.

One CAS attempt against one Git backend performs one checkpoint load and build. It does not rescan the checkpoint for each incoming session. Request preparation happens once before the retry loop. A CAS conflict causes one more load and build from the winning tip.

## Validation

`mise run check` passed on the committed tree. This included:

- formatting;
- golangci-lint with zero issues;
- the aggregate race-enabled unit and integration suite;
- Vogon, 56 of 56;
- roger-roger, 4 of 4.

Focused race-enabled tests also passed for:

- batch validation, ordering, summaries, timestamps, trailers, task collisions, and both Git layouts;
- concurrent metadata-ref and per-checkpoint-ref writes;
- SHA-1 and SHA-256 CAS;
- transaction retries and cancellation;
- initialization and migration;
- dispatch, kind routing, fanout, and filesystem storage;
- reconciliation, cleanup, ref advancement, rewind, and OPF publication;
- persistent-ref writer coverage.

The advisory duplication scan found nothing in `persistent_batch.go`. Its production persistent-backend findings come from older read-wrapper patterns. The only related new finding is duplicated routing-test setup.

No paid real-agent E2E tests were run.

## Left for the next PR

PostCommit still writes sessions one at a time. Completing #2091 item 2 requires the lifecycle layer to:

1. Group materialized `process_sessions` results by checkpoint ID.
2. Build one `BatchSessions` request per checkpoint.
3. Persist enough intent to recover after a process crash.
4. Submit one batch write per checkpoint.
5. Retry safely when one physical backend may already contain the batch.
6. Keep combined attribution as a separate transaction.
7. Remove completed intent only after every required primary write succeeds.
8. Define when stale intent can be removed without losing recoverable work.
9. Test interruption before publication, partial backend success, retry, and cleanup.
10. Re-run the commit-hook performance tests and confirm that checkpoint loading and building happen once per checkpoint.

Until that work lands, single-session writes are safer and use the shared builder, but the full `process_sessions` latency reduction is not active.

Task-v2 storage, attribution folding, unrelated CLI cleanup, and the existing commit-hook performance-test work remain out of scope.

## Review status

Stages 1 and 2 were reviewed independently. No Critical, High, or Medium correctness defect was found.

The remaining hardening ideas are non-blocking:

- Check cancellation again after acquiring the repository object lock.
- Replace the lexical persistent-ref writer inventory with an AST-based check.
- Narrow native Git’s `cannot lock ref` error classification if callers need more precise operational errors.
- Revisit process-lifetime lock-map retention if this code moves into a long-running process that repeatedly opens repositories.

Persistent checkpoint writers use a per-reference cross-process lock followed by native Git compare-and-swap. The two OPF rewrite paths still used go-git's `CheckAndSetReference`, which does not participate in native Git's reference locking protocol.

A native checkpoint update and an OPF rewrite could therefore both observe the same old value and both report success. When the native transaction committed, it overwrote the OPF result, silently losing an update.

## The fix

Add `checkpoint.CASPersistentRef`, which acquires the existing persistent-ref lock and performs the final compare-and-swap through native `git update-ref`. Route both OPF writers through it:

- the shared `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` rewrite
- per-checkpoint reference rewrites

The potentially expensive OPF scan remains outside the lock. If another writer advances the reference during that scan, the final native CAS rejects the stale rewrite instead of overwriting the newer value.

## Why this approach

Native Git CAS is the correctness boundary: it respects Git's reference locks and guarantees that only one writer can replace the expected old value.

We also acquire Entire's existing per-reference lock. This lets cooperating Entire processes wait for each other instead of producing avoidable conflicts, while native Git still protects against external Git processes.

Using native `git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>` without Entire's lock was another valid option. It would prevent lost updates, but concurrent Entire writers would fail immediately instead of coordinating through the protocol already used by persistent checkpoint writes.

Larger alternatives, such as centralizing all reference writes or changing go-git's locking behavior, could also solve the problem but would substantially expand the scope and risk of this fix. Using only Entire's lock with go-git would not be sufficient because external Git processes do not honor Entire's lock.

The deliberate behavior change is that an OPF rewrite may now briefly wait or fail safely with a conflict. It can no longer report success and then be silently overwritten.

## Verification

The regression tests start a real native `git update-ref --stdin` transaction, pause it after `prepare` while Git owns the reference lock, and then exercise each OPF rewrite path.

Before the fix, both tests demonstrated the lost-update window:

```text
Error: An error is expected but got nil.
Messages: the OPF rewrite must not report success while a native update owns the ref lock
```

After the fix, the focused regression tests passed ten times under the race detector:

```text
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint 2.034s
ok github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy 7.075s
```

`mise run check` also passed, including formatting, lint, race-enabled unit and integration tests, and the Vogon and Roger-Roger canary suites.

## Scope

This closes the two OPF call sites identified in #2204. Existing strategy reference writes used for initialization, recovery, and migration are unchanged.

Missing-ref creation passes the correct all-zero object ID in both SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories.

`RunRefTransaction` retries a logical mutation when another writer wins the race. Each attempt reads the current tip, rebuilds from that tip, and publishes with CAS. Conflicts use bounded, cancellation-aware jitter. The transaction stops after 16 attempts.

A mutation that reports `changed=false` is an idempotent no-op and does not call `git update-ref`.

The CAS conversion covers persistent v1 metadata refs and per-checkpoint refs, including:

- initial ref creation;
- v1 migration;
- attribution, summary, and transcript backfills;
- reconciliation and safe local ref advancement;
- orphan cleanup and expected-old deletion;
- shadow-branch migration;
- rewind publication;
- OPF publication.

OPF uses one CAS attempt by design. If its expected ref has moved, it fails closed and withholds the push. It does not rebuild sanitized output from newly appeared content.

- Every session must reference that checkpoint.
- Session IDs must be valid and unique.
- Sessions are sorted by `SessionID`.
- Task tool-use IDs and agent IDs must be valid.
- Duplicate task IDs within or across incoming sessions are rejected.
- Sessions without timestamps share one UTC timestamp, truncated to seconds.

For each CAS attempt, the builder:

- loads the existing checkpoint once;
- reads each existing session’s metadata once;
- reuses the numeric index when updating a session;
- preserves untouched session subtree hashes;
- appends new sessions in canonical order;
- merges the task subtree once and preserves untouched tasks;
- reduces the complete final session set into the root summary;
- preserves combined attribution and sticky review, investigation, and import flags;

0/transcript.jsonl
1/...

session entries visited       N
existing metadata reads       N
task entries visited          0
final-session contributions   N

- formatting;
- golangci-lint with zero issues;
- the aggregate race-enabled unit and integration suite;
- Vogon, 56 of 56;
- roger-roger, 4 of 4.

- transaction retries and cancellation;

index 000000000..4a2c0cbea

@@ -0,0 +1,69 @@
+package gitrepo
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"errors"
+	"fmt"
+	"os/exec"
+	"strings"
+
+	"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6/plumbing"
+)
+
+var (
+	// ErrRefCASConflict means the ref no longer has the expected old value.
+	ErrRefCASConflict = errors.New("git reference changed during compare-and-swap")
+	// ErrRefLocked means native Git could not acquire the ref lock.
+	ErrRefLocked = errors.New("git reference lock is unavailable")
+)
+
+// CompareAndSwapRef updates refName through native Git without dereferencing a
+// symbolic ref. ZeroHash as expectedHash requires that refName does not exist.
+func CompareAndSwapRef(
+	ctx context.Context,
+	repoRoot string,
+	refName plumbing.ReferenceName,
+	newHash, expectedHash plumbing.Hash,
+) error {
+	newValue := newHash.String()
+	oldValue := strings.Repeat("0", newHash.HexSize())
+	if expectedHash != plumbing.ZeroHash {
+		oldValue = expectedHash.String()
+	}
+
+	cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "update-ref", "--no-deref", "--end-of-options", refName.String(), newValue, oldValue)
+	cmd.Dir = repoRoot
+	cmd.Env = gitPlumbingEnv()
+	stderr, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
+	if err == nil {
+		return nil
+	}
+	if ctxErr := ctx.Err(); ctxErr != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("git update-ref %s: %w", refName, ctxErr)
+	}
+
+	detail := strings.TrimSpace(string(stderr))
+	switch {
+	case isRefCASConflict(stderr):
+		return fmt.Errorf("git update-ref %s: %s: %w", refName, detail, ErrRefCASConflict)
+	case isRefLockContention(stderr):
+		return fmt.Errorf("git update-ref %s: %s: %w", refName, detail, ErrRefLocked)
+	default:
+		return fmt.Errorf("git update-ref %s: %s: %w", refName, detail, err)
+	}
+}
+
+// isRefCASConflict reports that git rejected the expected old value, including
+// the cases where a required ref disappeared or a create-only ref appeared.
+func isRefCASConflict(stderr []byte) bool {
+	msg := strings.ToLower(string(stderr))
+	return strings.Contains(msg, "but expected") ||
+		strings.Contains(msg, "unable to resolve reference") ||
+		strings.Contains(msg, "reference already exists")
+}
+
+func isRefLockContention(stderr []byte) bool {
+	msg := strings.ToLower(string(stderr))
+	return strings.Contains(msg, "cannot lock references") ||
+		strings.Contains(msg, ".lock") && strings.Contains(msg, "file exists")
+}

+
+func TestOPFV1RewriteDoesNotLoseConcurrentCheckpointUpdate(t *testing.T) {
+	configureFakeOPF(t, &fakeOPFForRewrite{})
+	repoRoot, repo, oldTip := setupV1RepoInDir(t)
+	tree := emptyTreeHash(t, repo)
+	nativeTip := makeOrphanCommit(t, repo, tree, []plumbing.Hash{oldTip}, "native checkpoint write")
+	refName := plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(paths.MetadataBranchName)
+
+	commitNative := prepareNativeRefUpdate(t, repoRoot, refName, oldTip, nativeTip)
+	_, opfErr := RewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF(t.Context(), repo, "origin")
+	commitNative()
+
+	finalRef, err := repo.Reference(refName, true)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	require.Equal(t, nativeTip, finalRef.Hash())
+	var movedErr *V1RefMovedError
+	require.NotErrorAs(t, opfErr, &movedErr,
+		"a held lock does not prove that the ref moved")
+	require.ErrorIs(t, opfErr, gitrepo.ErrRefLocked,
+		"the OPF rewrite must report ref contention while a native update owns the ref lock")
+}
+
+func TestAtomicSetV1Ref_ReportsActualCASConflictAsMoved(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+	_, repo, oldTip := setupV1RepoInDir(t)
+	tree := emptyTreeHash(t, repo)
+	newTip := makeOrphanCommit(t, repo, tree, []plumbing.Hash{oldTip}, "OPF rewrite")
+	externalTip := makeOrphanCommit(t, repo, tree, []plumbing.Hash{oldTip}, "concurrent checkpoint write")
+	refName := plumbing.NewBranchReferenceName(paths.MetadataBranchName)
+	require.NoError(t, repo.Storer.SetReference(plumbing.NewHashReference(refName, externalTip)))
+
+	err := atomicSetV1Ref(t.Context(), repo, oldTip, newTip)
+
+	var movedErr *V1RefMovedError
+	require.ErrorAs(t, err, &movedErr)
+	require.Equal(t, &V1RefMovedError{Expected: oldTip, Actual: externalTip}, movedErr)
+	require.NotErrorIs(t, err, gitrepo.ErrRefLocked)
+}
+
+func TestOPFCheckpointRefRewriteDoesNotLoseConcurrentCheckpointUpdate(t *testing.T) {
+	configureFakeOPF(t, &fakeOPFForRewrite{})
+	_, repo, refs := setupGitRefsOPFRepo(t, "a1b2c3d4e5f6")
+	worktree, err := repo.Worktree()
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	repoRoot := worktree.Filesystem().Root()
+	refName := refs[0]
+	oldRef, err := repo.Reference(refName, true)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	oldCommit, err := repo.CommitObject(oldRef.Hash())
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	nativeTip := makeOrphanCommit(t, repo, oldCommit.TreeHash, []plumbing.Hash{oldRef.Hash()}, "native checkpoint write")
+
+	commitNative := prepareNativeRefUpdate(t, repoRoot, refName, oldRef.Hash(), nativeTip)
+	opfErr := RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF(t.Context(), repo)
+	commitNative()
+
+	finalRef, err := repo.Reference(refName, true)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	require.Equal(t, nativeTip, finalRef.Hash())
+	require.ErrorIs(t, opfErr, gitrepo.ErrRefLocked,
+		"the OPF rewrite must report ref contention while a native update owns the ref lock")
+}
+
+func prepareNativeRefUpdate(
+	t *testing.T,
+	repoRoot string,
+	refName plumbing.ReferenceName,
+	oldTip plumbing.Hash,
+	newTip plumbing.Hash,
+) func() {
+	t.Helper()
+	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(t.Context(), 10*time.Second)
+	cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "update-ref", "--stdin")
+	cmd.Dir = repoRoot
+	cmd.Env = testutil.GitIsolatedEnv()
+	stdin, err := cmd.StdinPipe()
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	stdout, err := cmd.StdoutPipe()
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	var stderr bytes.Buffer
+	cmd.Stderr = &stderr
+	require.NoError(t, cmd.Start())
+	t.Cleanup(func() {
+		cancel()
+		if cmd.ProcessState == nil {
+			if err := cmd.Wait(); err != nil {
+				t.Logf("stopped unfinished git update-ref transaction: %v", err)
+			}
+		}
+	})
+
+	scanner := bufio.NewScanner(stdout)
+	writeAndExpectGitUpdateRefResponse(t, stdin, scanner, "start", "start: ok")
+	writeAndExpectGitUpdateRefResponse(t, stdin, scanner,
+		fmt.Sprintf("update %s %s %s", refName, newTip, oldTip), "")
+	writeAndExpectGitUpdateRefResponse(t, stdin, scanner, "prepare", "prepare: ok")
+
+	return func() {
+		writeAndExpectGitUpdateRefResponse(t, stdin, scanner, "commit", "commit: ok")
+		require.NoError(t, stdin.Close())
+		waitErr := cmd.Wait()
+		require.NoError(t, waitErr, stderr.String())
+	}
+}
+
+func writeAndExpectGitUpdateRefResponse(
+	t *testing.T,
+	stdin io.Writer,
+	scanner *bufio.Scanner,
+	command string,
+	want string,
+) {
+	t.Helper()
+	_, err := fmt.Fprintln(stdin, command)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	if want == "" {
+		return
+	}
+	require.True(t, scanner.Scan(), "git update-ref ended before %q", want)
+	require.Equal(t, want, scanner.Text())
+}

 // returns the commits that do not carry the OPF trailer, ancestor-first, plus
 // the parent the deepest one keeps: the trailered commit the walk stopped at,
 // or zero at a root. Checkpoint refs are a single-parent chain, so the first
 // parent is the whole history.
 func unappliedAncestry(repo *git.Repository, tip plumbing.Hash) ([]*object.Commit, plumbing.Hash, error) {
 	var chain []*object.Commit
 	base := plumbing.ZeroHash
 	for h := tip; !h.IsZero(); {
 		c, err := repo.CommitObject(h)
 		if err != nil {
 			return nil, plumbing.ZeroHash, fmt.Errorf("load commit %s: %w", h.String()[:7], err)
 		}
 		if trailers.HasOPFApplied(c.Message) {
 			base = h
 			break
 		}
 		chain = append(chain, c)
 		if len(c.ParentHashes) == 0 {
 			break
 		}
 		h = c.ParentHashes[0]
 	}
 	slices.Reverse(chain)
 	return chain, base, nil
 }

{"body":"#1926 routed persistent checkpoint ref updates through a cross-process flock plus native `git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>`, which closed #1917 for the checkpoint store's own writers.

Two writers in `strategy` still update those same refs outside that lock, using go-git's `CheckAndSetReference`:

- `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go:815` - CAS on `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1`
- `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_opf_refs.go:169` - CAS on the per-checkpoint refs

Both compare-and-swap, so this is not the unconditional-update defect from #1917. The problem is that go-git's `CheckAndSetReference` does not interoperate with native git's `.lock` files - the reason documented at `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/shadow_ref.go:53`. So a pre-push OPF rewrite and a post-commit condensation can now race on the same ref through two mutually invisible CAS mechanisms.

The author of #1926 called this out in that PR's description as remaining scope.

Needs its own reproduction before a fix - #1917's does not cover it, since both sides here verify an expected old value.
","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2204","state":"open","title":"OPF writers still CAS checkpoint refs via go-git, racing #1926's native update-ref"}

{"author":"MuskanPaliwal","body":"Hey @Soph , Thanks for flagging this. Before I resolve the overlap, this is the shape I’m planning.

#2131 already has the first two parts of the batching work:

- A shared ref transaction API that reads the current tip, rebuilds against it, and publishes with native Git CAS.
- A `BatchSessions` storage request and shared builder for both `git-branch` and `git-refs`.

The storage-level batching is implemented. It can load one checkpoint, upsert several sessions, recompute the summary once, build one commit, and publish it once. Single-session writes also use that builder.

What #2131 does not do yet is use `BatchSessions` from `PostCommit`. The `process_sessions` loop still calls `CondenseSession` once per session, and each call writes one `ReservedSession`. That lifecycle change is planned for Stage 3.

The direct overlap with #1926 is the persistent-ref transaction code. Both PRs implement native CAS, retry, and rebuild behavior around many of the same writers. #1926 also adds some behavior that #2131 currently lacks:

- A cross-process filesystem lock for each persistent ref.
- Context-aware waiting for the lock.
- Holding the lock across the full read, build, CAS, and retry cycle.
- Cleaning up a losing commit only after a confirmed CAS conflict.
- The concurrent two-Stop-hook integration regression.

My plan is to keep #2131’s transaction API rather than carry `persistent_ref_update.go` forward as a second implementation. I would move #1926’s guarantees into `RunRefTransaction` and the multi-ref transaction path.

The result should work like this:

- The transaction acquires #1926’s per-ref filesystem lock before reading the tip.
- It holds the lock while building and publishing the commit.
- Native Git CAS remains the final publication check.
- If an external writer bypasses Entire’s lock and moves the ref, the transaction rereads the winning tip and rebuilds.
- Multi-ref transactions acquire all required ref locks in a fixed order before using the atomic multi-ref CAS path.
- Losing commits are removed only after confirmed CAS conflicts. Hard errors preserve them because Git may already have published the ref.

The process-local mutex in #2131 and the filesystem lock from #1926 have different jobs. The mutex protects go-git object construction from goroutines in one CLI process. The filesystem lock coordinates separate Entire processes. Git CAS protects the final ref update, including against tools that do not use Entire’s lock.

I would also keep the intent of #1926’s tests. Cooperating Entire writers should serialize on the filesystem lock. A simulated external Git writer should bypass the lock and exercise the CAS retry path. The concurrent Stop-hook integration regression should remain as end-to-end coverage.

Stage 3 would keep this locking. It would group prepared sessions by checkpoint ID and submit one `BatchSessions` write, so the persistent-ref lock is acquired once for the checkpoint batch instead of once per session. The remaining Stage 3 work is in the lifecycle: preparing sessions without immediately writing them, durable recovery intent, state finalization after publication, partial-backend retries, attribution, telemetry, and safe shadow-branch cleanup.

So the merge rule I’m proposing is: keep #2131’s transaction and batching structure, but carry #1926’s locking, cleanup, cancellation, and concurrency guarantees into that structure.
","created_at":"2026-09-01T06:43:08Z","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2131#issuecomment-5489979780"}
{"author":"MuskanPaliwal","body":"Pushed a follow-up in [15427c7b1](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2211/commits/15427c7b100bd55b2c5e8ed5e92402e463c21aae) for the review findings. The ref CAS now lives in one place, uses `--no-deref`, and tells a stale ref apart from a held lock. Persistent writers retry when the ref disappears, and flock waits now stop on cancellation even without a deadline. I also added real loose-ref and reftable contention tests, plus coverage through the public OPF paths.

`mise run check` passes, including race tests, integration tests, and the deterministic canaries. Ready for another look.","created_at":"2026-09-01T10:28:45Z","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2211#issuecomment-5492574776"}
{"author":"Soph","body":"#2131 and #2211 both convert the two OPF call sites to native CAS, through two different APIs. `git merge-tree` on the current heads conflicts in six files, including a modify/delete on `persistent_ref_update.go`, which #2131 removes and this PR extends.

What do you want to carry forward?
","created_at":"2026-09-01T11:22:12Z","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2211#issuecomment-5493155727"}

{"body":"#1926 routed persistent checkpoint ref updates through a cross-process flock plus native `git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>`, which closed #1917 for the checkpoint store's own writers.

Two writers in `strategy` still update those same refs outside that lock, using go-git's `CheckAndSetReference`:

- `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go:815` - CAS on `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1`
- `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_opf_refs.go:169` - CAS on the per-checkpoint refs

Both compare-and-swap, so this is not the unconditional-update defect from #1917. The problem is that go-git's `CheckAndSetReference` does not interoperate with native git's `.lock` files - the reason documented at `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/shadow_ref.go:53`. So a pre-push OPF rewrite and a post-commit condensation can now race on the same ref through two mutually invisible CAS mechanisms.

The author of #1926 called this out in that PR's description as remaining scope.

Needs its own reproduction before a fix - #1917's does not cover it, since both sides here verify an expected old value.

The storage-level batching is implemented. It can load one checkpoint, upsert several sessions, recompute the summary once, build one commit, and publish it once. Single-session writes also use that builder.

What #2131 does not do yet is use `BatchSessions` from `PostCommit`. The `process_sessions` loop still calls `CondenseSession` once per session, and each call writes one `ReservedSession`. That lifecycle change is planned for Stage 3.

The direct overlap with #1926 is the persistent-ref transaction code. Both PRs implement native CAS, retry, and rebuild behavior around many of the same writers. #1926 also adds some behavior that #2131 currently lacks:

- A cross-process filesystem lock for each persistent ref.
- Context-aware waiting for the lock.
- Holding the lock across the full read, build, CAS, and retry cycle.

Stage 3 would keep this locking. It would group prepared sessions by checkpoint ID and submit one `BatchSessions` write, so the persistent-ref lock is acquired once for the checkpoint batch instead of once per session. The remaining Stage 3 work is in the lifecycle: preparing sessions without immediately writing them, durable recovery intent, state finalization after publication, partial-backend retries, attribution, telemetry, and safe shadow-branch cleanup.

So the merge rule I’m proposing is: keep #2131’s transaction and batching structure, but carry #1926’s locking, cleanup, cancellation, and concurrency guarantees into that structure.

content.text:
The facts support keeping #2131 as the production implementation and treating #2211 only as a source of tests and hardening.

What I found:

- #2131 already converts both OPF publication sites to `checkpoint.CompareAndSwapRef`:

  - `RewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF`
  - `RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF`

- #2131 deliberately deletes `persistent_ref_update.go` and centralizes persistent writes in `ref_transaction.go`.
- #2211 instead extends `persistent_ref_update.go` with `CASPersistentRef`, creating the duplicate API Soph flagged.
- The six merge conflicts are:

  1. `checkpoint/ephemeral_test.go`
  2. `checkpoint/persistent_ref_update.go` — modify/delete
  3. `checkpoint/persistent_ref_update_test.go` — modify/delete
  4. `checkpoint/shadow_ref.go`
  5. `strategy/manual_commit_opf_refs.go`
  6. `strategy/manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go`

There is also an unpublished local follow-up on the #2131 branch:

- Commit `05feaacd` — `fix(checkpoint): restore cross-process ref locking`
- It keeps `persistent_ref_update.go` deleted.
- It moves the per-ref filesystem lock into `RunRefTransaction`.
- It acquires multi-ref locks in sorted order.
- It holds locks across read, build, CAS, and retry.
- It adds conflict-only cleanup of losing commits.
- The local `improve-process-sessions-condensation` branch contains this commit, but GitHub’s #2131 head is still `56e583e0`, so Soph cannot see it yet.

What #2211 uniquely contributes and is worth carrying into #2131:

- End-to-end reproductions for both OPF paths using a real prepared native `git update-ref` transaction.
- Separate classification of:

  - stale expected value;
  - native ref-lock contention;
  - unrelated ref namespace failures.

- `--no-deref` protection.
- The `AcquireContext` fix for cancellation without a deadline. This matters because #2131’s local locking follow-up calls `AcquireContext`, while the older implementation only honors contexts with deadlines.

What should not be carried:

- `CASPersistentRef`.
- `persistent_ref_update.go` or its tests as a separate abstraction.
- The separate `gitrepo/ref_cas.go` ownership seam if native CAS remains owned by `checkpoint/ref_transaction.go`.
- The OPF call-site changes themselves—they already exist in #2131.

One semantic wrinkle: #2131 currently classifies native lock contention as `ErrRefConflict`. Consequently, the v1 OPF path may report `V1RefMovedError` with identical expected and actual hashes when the ref merely remained locked. That is safe—no update is lost—but misleading. #2211 fixes that distinction, so the classification improvement should be ported into #2131’s transaction API.

My recommended answer to Soph is:

> Keep #2131’s `ref_transaction.go` and batching structure; do not carry `CASPersistentRef` or restore `persistent_ref_update.go`. I already have a local #2131 follow-up that moves the cross-process locking and conflict cleanup into the transaction API. From #2211, I want to carry the two public OPF concurrency regressions, `--no-deref`, precise stale-vs-lock error classification, and the cancel-without-deadline flock fix, implemented within #2131’s transaction structure. Once those are on #2131, #2211’s production implementation is superseded.

No code or branch state was changed during this research.

# Draft GitHub Reply

Prepare paste-ready GitHub text without publishing it. A comment, review, issue,
or PR update is an external communication made in the user's name, so drafting
and publishing are separate decisions.

## Non-Negotiable Contract

1. Treat every initial request involving a GitHub reply or comment as
   **draft-only**, including wording such as "comment on this issue," "post my
   reply," "respond there," or "reply to the maintainer."
2. Do not call any write-capable GitHub command or API while drafting. This
   includes `gh issue comment`, `gh pr comment`, `gh pr review`, `gh api` with a
   mutating method, GraphQL mutations, or equivalent browser actions.
3. Read-only inspection is allowed when useful: inspect the issue, PR, linked
   comment, reviews, and local code to understand context.
4. Return only the proposed reply unless the user also asks for analysis. Do
   not preface it with a plan or discussion of what the reply will say.
5. After presenting the draft, wait. Do not publish it in the same turn.
6. Publish only when a later user message explicitly approves that exact draft
   and explicitly instructs publication, for example:
   - "Post that exact draft."
   - "Approved, publish it on issue #123."
   - "Use the second version and post it."
7. Treat revisions as a new draft. If the user changes wording, present the
   revised text and wait for fresh explicit approval before publishing.
8. Approval to publish one draft applies only to the named destination and
   exact text. Do not reuse it for another PR, issue, review, or comment.
9. If approval or the destination is ambiguous, ask one short clarifying
   question instead of publishing.

## Output

When only a draft is requested, output the paste-ready text with no quotation
marks and no extra explanation. If context or assumptions materially affect the
wording, put a short note after the draft, not before it.

When the user explicitly asks to understand a maintainer's point as well as
draft a response, use:

**Draft**

[paste-ready reply]

**Interpretation**

[concise explanation]

The interpretation is for the user and must not be included in a later posted
comment unless the user explicitly approves it as part of the draft.

## Examples

Initial request: "Comment on this issue and explain what the maintainer means."

Action: inspect read-only context, provide a draft and interpretation, and do
not post.

Initial request: "Post a reply saying the fix is ready."

Action: draft the reply only. The word "post" in the initial request does not
authorize publication.

Follow-up: "That looks good."

Action: do not post because this approves quality but does not explicitly
instruct publication. Wait or ask whether the user wants it published.

Follow-up: "Post that exact draft on PR #42."

Action: publication is authorized for that exact draft on PR #42 only.

Thanks for flagging the overlap. I want #2131 to remain the source of truth for this work because its `ref_transaction.go` API is the foundation for the batching implementation.

My intended merge rule is:

- Keep #2131’s ref transaction and batching structure.
- Keep `persistent_ref_update.go` deleted; I do not want to carry `CASPersistentRef` forward as a second transaction API.
- Move the useful guarantees into #2131’s transaction structure: per-ref cross-process locking, context-aware lock acquisition, native Git CAS, retry-and-rebuild behavior, deterministic multi-ref lock ordering, and cleanup only after a confirmed conflict.
- Keep OPF as a one-attempt, fail-closed publication rather than rebuilding sanitized output after the expected ref has moved.
- Carry forward #2211’s OPF-specific regression coverage for both the v1 metadata ref and per-checkpoint refs.
- Carry forward the smaller CAS hardening from #2211—particularly `--no-deref`, distinguishing a stale expected value from temporary native lock contention, and cancellation without a context deadline—but implement it within #2131’s transaction design rather than preserving the competing API.

I described the proposed combined design in more detail in [my latest comment on #2131](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2131#issuecomment-5489979780). In particular, that comment explains how I intend the process-local object mutex, cross-process filesystem lock, and native Git CAS to have separate responsibilities, and how the same structure extends to multi-ref transactions and eventual checkpoint-level batching.

Could you review that design on #2131 before I reconcile the branches? I would especially appreciate confirmation that moving the locking and cleanup guarantees into `RunRefTransaction` and its multi-ref counterpart is the shape you want. Once we agree on that ownership boundary, I can reduce #2211 to the OPF-specific tests and hardening that are still missing, or close it as superseded after those pieces are incorporated into #2131.
